Mr. Speaker, a Manotick physician has been cleared of sexual assault charges concerning a 21-year-old female patient in the emergency ward of his hospital.
Anyone making a study of recent publications on the subject will discover that the veil of silence on this taboo-physicians sexually abusing their female patients-is being raised.
In the case of the patient from Perth, an attempt was made to show that, far from calming her, the Valium prescribed by her physician had been the source of a libidinous perception.
Mr. Speaker, since when is Valium a stimulant, given the fact that evidence gathered over a number of years proves that the depressive conditions of many women can be traced back to this drug?
Allow me to question the soundness of comments on Valium. Even the judge has stated that he still entertains reasonable doubts in his mind.

September 17, 1987
What more do we need, what kind of evidence must be submitted when we know that the facts which were corroborated are the same as those which are accepted in cases of sexual abuse of children by adults?
So when will justice prevail in cases of sexual abuse against women, and what more de we need to make judges fully aware of this approach?

Law enforcement officers have faced a task of tremendous proportions in their efforts to crack down on the drug trade. The National Drug Strategy and, in particular, the new legislation to confiscate the proceeds of crime have at last provided Canadian enforcement officers with the resources and tools to confront and to overcome the growing danger that drug abuse poses to society. New initiatives in public education, treatment and rehabilitation, law enforcement and research, will provide an effective and comprehensive offensive against drug abuse.
1 call upon all Canadians and all Members of the House to put aside partisan politics and support the Government in the fight against drugs.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Conference to Observe the International Year of Shelter for the Homeless ended its deliberations in Ottawa yesterday. This conference heard firsthand about the crisis of homelessness here in Canada and, indeed, around the world.
In 1982, when the United Nations designated 1987 as the International Year of Shelter for the Homeless, one of the objectives was to have every country achieve a measure of improvement in the actual living conditions of those who are at the low end of the income scale. Today, there is every indication that in Canada conditions are even worse than they were in 1982.
There is no doubt at all that homelessness and the risk of being homeless are affecting a greater number of Canadians today than at any time since the Great Depression. The crisis crosses all segments of our society and impacts most heavily on women, natives, young people and the poor.
The Government's obligation to this international year did not end when the conference concluded. The problem was known to it before it was highlighted by this conference. What is needed now is action and the political will to ensure that homes for the homeless become a right and not simply a commodity on which a profit can be made.

Mr. Speaker, a couple of days ago over 500 people converged on Parliament Hill to protest the lack of shelter that 12,000 or more Canadians face every night. In this the International Year of Shelter for the Homeless we must try to come to terms with this national tragedy.
The plight of the homeless and the poor goes to the core of the issue of human dignity and the right to the basics of life. Deprived of acceptable lodging and adequate food, how can the poor feel that they are an integral part of a developed and humanitarian society?
Soup kitchens, churches and charitable organizations have been left with the burden of helping the needy in our society. It is time that all Canadians and, in particular, all Governments, especially the national Government of Canada, help out and take part in ending what has become a national disgrace.

Mr. Speaker, drug abuse is a growing problem in Canada, a problem which affects all segments of society. RCMP drug intelligence reports that the number of major cocaine traffickers is increasing and that the use of potent cocaine derivatives and combinations with other substances is becoming more prevalent, while domestic production of cannabis and chemical drugs is on the rise.

subsubtopic: SIGNING OF INTERNATIONAL PROTOCOL ON MEASURES TO PROTECT OZONE LAYER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), and the representatives of 43 other countries who drafted an international agreement yesterday. This agreement will help to preserve the earth's ozone layer, the protective layer of gases which shields the earth from the harmful rays of the sun.
September 17, 1987

This agreement comes none too soon. Already there are huge holes in the ozone layer over the Arctic and the Antarctic. Without controls on those chemicals which destroy the ozone layer, the problem will begin to move further into countries like Canada. A depletion in the ozone layer could have a devastating impact on agricultural production in this country, changing weather patterns, and turning the Prairies into a vast desert. Other results would be a significant increase in cases of skin cancer and eye disease.
The successful negotiation of this treaty is proof of the continuing role of the United Nations in establishing international environmental agreements. It is also an indication of the growing awareness of most, if not all Governments that the environment must be preserved in order that future generations will be able to enjoy a healthy environment on this planet, an environment which all too often we take for granted.

Mr. Speaker, one of the most misunderstood women's health issues is menopause, and the aging process which brings fears of osteoporosis. This week at two separate health conferences the use of the female hormone estrogen for treatment of women was raised.
The Osteoporosis Society of Canada claims that estrogen is a safe and effective way for selected women to prevent the debilitating bone disease osteoporosis. At another conference a radically different message was delivered that women can safely thwart the natural aging process by using estrogen treatment. This message presumes that menopause is the end of health, vigour, attractiveness, and libido, and that women should seek to remain adolescent beauties all their lives.
I applaud Dr. Joan Harrison who said, "I think staying young is an attitude of mind, and keeping fit and alive and active and interested in life is far more important than any agent".
Let us have more research into the opportunities to age healthfully and gracefully, and less poppycock based on sexist stereotypes of female beauty.

Mr. Speaker, once again the cries are being heard clear across Canada for extensive reform of the criminal justice system in
our country. These cries for reform are well founded and deserving of serious attention from all Members of the House.
A report recently released by the National Parole Board indicates that in the last 12 years 130 killings have been committed by prisoners who were on parole or who were under mandatory supervision. In a recent and absolutely appalling incident the Parole Board issued an individual, serving a 10-year sentence, a one-day parole pass in order that he could celebrate a special personal occasion. On the same day of his release this individual appears to have committed murder, and two additional serious crimes.
How many lives must be taken, and how many more families must be destroyed before we, as the lawmakers of the country, take concrete	action	to reform	this shamefully
ineffective collection of pacifist nonsense we call our justice system?
In Medicine Hat, Alberta, a family is suffering because of our inept system and	our	failure	to deal with	the premeditatedrepeat murderers. I	for	one will continue	to fight for the
reinstatement of capital punishment and a proper justice system.

subsubtopic: MIGRATORY BIRDS CONVENTION ACT-EFFECT OF ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, aboriginal rights to hunt, fish, trap and gather were confirmed by the Royal Proclamation of 1763 which is now part of the Constitution, and guaranteed in the treaties signed with Indian First Nations. Those treaties are also recognized and affirmed in the Constitution.
Over the years these rights have been eroded by certain laws, including the Migratory Birds Convention Act, a convention between Canada and the United States.
In a judgment given on May 13, 1987, in the provincial court at The Pas, Manitoba, Judge William R. Martin stated:
In my opinion the Migratory Birds Convention Act cannot be used to extinguish the Indian's right to hunt migratory birds for food at all seasons. To the extent that the Migratory Birds Convention Act is inconsistent with the Constitution-it has no force and effect.
Therefore I call upon the Government of Canada to bring to an immediate end the harassment by RCMP officers of Indian persons in the James Bay area of northern Ontario, whose treaty and constitutional rights are being denied through enforcement of the Migratory Birds Convention Act.

September 17, 1987

subsubtopic: TELEVISION-EMMY AWARD FOR CANADIAN TECHNOLOGICAL ACHIEVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with the greatest pleasure that I rise to inform Hon. Members that last night in New York the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) accepted, on behalf of the Department of Communications, an Emmy Award for technological achievement in television.
This award was for technology that pioneered the use of small low-cost antennae, which provided services to remote communities in the Canadian North.
Today there are 14 North American satellites using this technology all over the continent-in Canada, the United States, and Mexico.
In fact it seems as if everybody is using this technology now. However, nobody would be doing so if a small number of enterprising Canadians had not been willing to accept the risk, the risk that had to be taken, to show the world that this technology could work. It shows what Canadian ingenuity, backed by a far-seeing research program, can accomplish.
I believe that all of us in the House can be justifiably proud of this noteworthy achievement and of the Canadian scientists and officials who made it possible.

subsubtopic: NUCLEAR WEAPONS-POSSIBILITY OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN UNITED STATES AND SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the talks in Washington this week between the Soviets and Americans on an arms agreement eliminating medium and short-range nuclear missiles are very heartening. A treaty may well be worked out by the end of the year.
We are encouraged, too, by Mr. Gorbachev's proposal that a United Nations mechanism be created for monitoring compliance with arms control accords. This is very much in line with Canadian proposals in the past, and we look forward to hearing the Minister's response when he addresses the U.N. next Tuesday.
Lest we get carried away, however, we must remind ourselves that enormous arsenals of strategic nuclear arms remain, arsenals capable of destroying the planet many times over, and growing daily in technological sophistication and offensive capabilities.
When will we see a halt to the growth in such weapons as air and submarine-launched Cruise missiles? When will we see massive reductions in all strategic offensive arms? When will we see the end of SDI?
What is happening in Washington this week is a prelude, an important prelude but still a prelude, to the enormous tasks that lie ahead.

subsubtopic: FUTURE OF WILNO, ONT., POST OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hamlet of Wilno in the County of Renfrew is the oldest community of Polish origin in Canada. The post office is in the general store and Rural Route No. 1, Wilno, originates in that location.
Canada Post wants to take the postmaster off salary and replace this position with a contract which will give the postmaster a commission on the sale of stamps, money orders, et cetera. She will receive about 83 cents an hour on a really heavy day.
The National Camp Grounds of the 400,000 Canadians of Polish origin in Canada, named Kaszuby, is just six miles from Wilno, and people come there from all over Canada.
Both the community of Wilno and the Canadian Polish Congress of Canada want the post office retained as is, with Rural Route No. 1, Wilno, kept intact.
The people of Wilno have asked me to tell the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) that they are insulted and angry at his Conservative Government's action.
In a letter to the Chairman of Canada Post Corporation, the President of the Canadian Polish Congress states:
The closing down of the Wilno community post office would be interpreted
as an insult not only to the people of that community, but to all Canadians of
Polish descent.
In the name of Canadian history, and in the name of Canadian heritage, I call upon the Prime Minister to call off the wolves and leave the Wilno post office alone.

subsubtopic: ACCORD ON REDUCTION OF CHEMICAL PRODUCTS DESTROYING OZONE SHIELD IN STRATOSPHERE
speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, more than 50 countries signed a treaty aimed at reducing by half the chemical products which destroy the ozone layer in the stratosphere. "For the first time in history we now have a global treaty under which the nations of the world have decided to take very specific measures to reduce the production of a product harmful to the environment." This statement was
September 17, 1987

made by Mr. Winfried Lang who chaired the September 8-to-16 conference held in Montreal under the aegis of the United Nations Environment Program. According to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan): "The treaty shows that countries can indeed afford to forget about their diverging views in their quest for a common goal-the preservation of life on earth".
Last April the World Commission on Environment and Development released a report linking international economic and environmental needs.
We have just been witness to the seriousness with which Canada and other countries take this link.
We must commend the Minister of the Environment and all others who worked hard towards the signature of this important treaty which is the kind of tool we need to protect our planet.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, on September 12, 1977, Stephen Biko, the heroic advocate of black independence in South Africa, died of savage injuries sustained while in police custody. Ten years later little has changed.
This week in the South African Parliament two proposals are being debated. One offers blacks throughout the country the opportunity to elect their own representatives to a National Advisory Council, and the other is a report on changes to the Group Areas Act which is the basis of residential segregation. The first has been rejected by black leaders. The second appears to be a token gesture.
Black leaders such as Oliver Tambo, Alan Boesak and Thabo Mbeki have repeatedly called for comprehensive and mandatory sanctions and a break in diplomatic ties, although this might mean isolation.
Now is the time to step up the pressure on South Africa before it is too late.

Mr. Speaker, today marks the third anniversary of the swearing in of the Mulroney
Oral Questions
administration. The quantity and significance of the legislation introduced and passed by this Government is without parallel in the history of Canadian federal politics.
The employment and economic record since September, 1984, is nothing short of remarkable. Nine hundred and seven thousand new jobs have been created; 88 per cent of these new jobs are full-time. There were more newspaper pages devoted to help-wanted ads in July of this year than at any point during the past 25 years. Interest rates have fallen 3 per cent. Five-year mortgages are down 2.75 per cent. Housing starts are up 86 per cent. Consumer spending has increased 32 per cent. Inflation is steady at 4 per cent. The deficit has declined in three consecutive years for the first time in 30 years.
Indeed, our economic growth now exceeds that of all major western industrialized nations. The Government has contributed to this outstanding economic growth by sensible policies on deficit and spending controls, deregulation, and foreign investment. It has also laid the foundation for continued growth by its leadership and vision in pursuing freer trade with the United States, and tax reform.
I admit that we, as a Government, have made some mistakes. However, no one can deny the outstanding record of these past three years.

Mr. Ronald Atkey, head of the Security Intelligence Review Committee, has indicated that as soon as he heard of Mr. Marc Boivin's connections with our security services the review office began an inquiry into the matter which has now extended to a number of trade unions in Canada. speechtext:

September 17, 1987

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can tell the Hon. Member, as he well knows, that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act permits CSIS to investigate anybody who is a security threat to Canada. Member is talking as if the review by Mr. Atkey's committee has already arrived at and finalized its conclusions and that what he is suggesting is in fact true. That is not the case.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House suspended the sitting at one o'clock the Hon. Member for Portneuf (Mr. Ferland) had the floor.

I was saying before lunch that the second initiative began in September 1985 when a second consultative group started to address the problems associated with the management of all aspects of toxic chemicals in order to minimize risks to human health and the environment while supporting industrial productivity and competiveness. This committee developed a report entitled "From Cradle to Grave: A Management Approach to Chemicals". This report establishes the "life-cycle" concept as the key analytical tool for managing chemicals as they proceed from their creation through research and development efforts, are introduced to the market place, manufactured, transported, distributed, used and, eventually, disposed of.
The draft legislation before us incorporates many of the recommendations contained in these two committee reports. We accept the principle that we must have measures to anticipate and prevent the problems of environmental contamination as well as be prepared to remedy harm when it has been done.
To this end the following provisions of the draft legislation are notable.
A brand new provision has been included to deal with the beginning of the life-cycle of a chemical: a strict regulatory program is proposed that would require industry to notify the federal government when a chemical substance is going to be manufactured in or imported into Canada for the first time. Sufficient information would be provided to clearly identify the chemical and to allow scientists within the Department of the Environment and the Department of National Health and Welfare to carry out a preliminary assessment of the potential of the chemical to create a health or environmental threat. This program would allow Canada to live up to international commitments made at the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. The details of this proposed scheme were developed by the consultative committee under the Environmental Contaminants Act and have the support of representatives of both industry and public interest groups and should merit the support of all members of this House.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
To complement the proposed measures for "new" chemicals, is a series of measures designed to cope with the problems associated with the thousands of chemicals currently in use in our society. The draft Environmental Protection Act would obligate the Minister of the Environment to develop and publicize a list of chemicals that would be assessed for health and environmental hazards on a priority basis. Any member of the public could make representations to the Minister of the Environment to include specific chemicals on the Priority List and the Minister must reply to each request. This system would provide for strong public input and accountability for the process of selecting chemicals for review. As hazard assessments are completed, they must be made public and all decisions to regulate or not to regulate a chemical will be open to an appeal process. This procedure for selecting and assessing chemicals should maintain public participation and restore the public's confidence that the Federal Government is making a timely and appropriate response to the potential threats posed by the chemicals that have become an integral part of our life in this country.
One of the purposes of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act is to control toxic chemicals in Canada. This draft legislation contains provisions to regulate virtually any of the foreseeable events in the life of a toxic chemical. In addition to the provisions 1 have already mentioned for controlling the entry of new chemicals to Canada, controls could be placed on the use, manufacture, import, release or disposal of toxic substances.
If toxic substances are imported, manufactured or distributed in contravention of any of the provisions of the Act, a recall, and possibly disposal, of all products containing the substance could be required by the Minister of the Environment. This type of provision is not found in any other current federal legislation and should encourage industry to comply with regulatory provisions of the Act and thus to prevent the contamination of our environment.
Another new provision would give the Federal Government the power to intervene when a spill or release of a toxic chemical is imminent or has occurred. This measure is designed to minimize or, hopefully, prevent damage to the environment that may be caused by the sudden release of large quantities of chemicals that are commonly used at industrial sites. This is another example of the kind of anticipatory measures that are part and parcel of a comprehensive cradle-to-grave approach to managing chemicals.
Mr. Speaker, as we attempt to protect the Canadian environment, we must realize that we are part of an international community. The ongoing international conference on ozone in Montreal is a prime example of the necessity for collective action on some environmental problems. We now recognize that some chemicals have the physical or chemical characteristics that allow them to become distributed about this planet of ours regardless of the original localized area of their use.

September 17, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Recognizing this need for international cooperation, the draft Environmental Protection Act contains a measure that would require Canadian industry to notify foreign countries if a toxic chemical listed under the Act is to be exported. This practice should ensure that recipients of Canadian exports are aware that we have regulated a chemical and the reasons why we have done so and, thus, can evaluate the need for any measures they may deem necessary. There are many international aspects to controlling the hazards of existing chemicals and an important part of implementing this new Act involves Canadian participation as a leader in such organizations as the World Health Organization, the United Nations Environment Program and the Organization for Enonomic Cooperation and Development.
Mr. Speaker. The current laws for protection of the environment from toxic chemicals were conceived in the social, political and scientific milieu of the late 1960's and early 1970's. We have learned a lot over the past 20 years-a good deal of that from our failure to cope successfully with the insidious and ever-present problems of environmental contamination.
Mr. Speaker, there is no need to recall the lethargy and apathy of our Liberal predecessors, and the complicity of our NDP colleagues, there is no need to recall how these people failed to live up to their responsibilities; aware at the time of the existence of certain very important files, denouncing a wide variety of chemical products, that Liberal government propped up by the New Democrats never did anything to curb this scourge. The people of Canada are demanding a stronger and more effective approach to prevent the contamination of our environment by the chemicals we have collectively chosen to live with in our society.
We have employed a novel approach over the last three years, involving representatives of the various sectors of our society in the development of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. While this Act deals with other threats to the environment, those portions relating to toxic chemicals assessment and control are, I believe, comprehensive, forward looking, and with the support of the members of this House, should be implemented in a timely fashion. These measures should help us progress to the twenty-first century in such a manner that we can assert to our children that we have not misused their inheritance, Mr. Speaker, and not the kind of inheritance which you and I and the whole Government were left with when we came here in September 1984, faced as we were with the consequences of the outright apathy of the previous administration which had never had the gumption to get a handle on such serious issues as that of the environment.
Mr. Speaker, this morning I heard Opposition Members say that this Government has not done anything. In the course of my remarks I indicated that we began to deal with environmental problems as early as in February 1985. With respect to acid rain our Government signed agreements with the seven provinces which were the worst offenders in terms of acid pollutant emissions. We did manage to conclude an agreement
with the Government of Quebec, something which our predecessors had always deemed unthinkable, unworkable. Well, this Government and this Minister did manage to negotiate an agreement under which it will be possible to reduce acid fallout by 50 per cent in Quebec. That is the kind of constructive measures we took.
I realize that my time is very limited, but still I would like to highlight the efforts of this Government to enhance the environment. We have now been in office for three years, and I believe we have created the highest number of parks in this country, more than ever before in the last hundred years, if I am not mistaken. Recent announcements were made concerning South Moresby Park in British Columbia, Ellesmere in the Northwest Territories, Bruce in Ontario. More projects are on the negotiation table and the Minister is committed to develop marine parks. All these initiatives to protect the environment reflect the commitment which our Government, our Minister and our Prime Minister have always advocated to show that we as a Government, as Members of the Progressive Conservative Party, are intent on leaving as a legacy for our children an environment which will be in better condition than what we found on September 4, 1984 when the people gave us a very specific mandate: first, to try to set the Canadian economy on an even keel and, second, to try to repair the damage which had been done to the environment.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of the Hon. Member. I agree it is a good first step in this very complicated subject of toxins which change frequently with new technology. It is an area with which we have to keep up. I certainly laud the sentiments and the commitments which the Hon. Member sees as reflected in the Bill.
Could he comment on the enforcement aspects? We have seen many attempts made with good intentions, but it is very difficult unless things are well enforced.

Mr. Speaker, about the same question was asked to one of my colleagues this morning. The Minister has stated that it is not enough to introduce this Bill, even though it is quite impressive and important, as well as a first in Canada, contains clear commitments and also provides for very clear penalties, because we also need the means to implement it. Hon. Members will recall that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) made such a commitment and mentioned new funds of $37 million. This was not an empty promise as action has already been taken. We have taken action and showed some courage while our predecessors never had the courage to face Canadian businesses and polluters and tell them: Enough is enough! Hon. Members should recognize that we have had that courage.
The new Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) has at least had the courage, with her Party, to recognize that we have
September 17, 1987

made these efforts, but I have to remind the Elouse that we need more money. We also have to remember the last agreements signed in relation with acid rain, another pollutant which attacks not only our forests, but also the water resources which are the very basis of survival on this planet. We have signed agreements with the private sector and the Quebec Government and we have decreased substantially the level of acid rain.

Mr. Speaker, I know the Eton. Member is a very knowledgeable Member on environmental affairs. Although this Bill does not deal with the issue of acid rain, a number of speakers from the Official Opposition have indicated that during the past three years the Government has not taken any steps whatsoever with respect to the environment, apart from the introduction of this one Bill.
I believe the Hon. Member is a member of the House committee on acid rain. He has outlined a few of the things the Government has been doing in the area of acid rain. I know he is aware that 50 per cent of the acid rain emissions that cause problems in Canada originate here and the other 50 per cent originate in the United States. I know he is aware as well that this is the very first Government that has placed the question of acid rain as a first priority in discussions between the United States and Canada. I believe the Member was in Washington not too long ago in an effort to try to convince Americans to take some action in this respect.
Would he outline to the House, particularly for those in the Official Opposition, who do not seem to be aware of the efforts that have been taken respecting the environment and other issues, some of the steps that have been taken and what progress is being made?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for York East (Mr. Redway). People often have the impression that those who are concerned with environmental problems live mostly in rural areas. However, my colleague is from the city, and I appreciate the interest he has always shown for the quality of our environment. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is essential for Members of Parliament representing urban areas to become more aware of this issue. I went to Washington with my colleagues of the Committee on Acid Rain to make the American legislators aware of their responsibility to their good Northern neighbours, as they like to call us. I must say that we had very serious meetings. I believe that the American Senators and Congressmen saw in our comments a very firm will on our part to have them develop policies similar to those applied in Canada. We clearly told them that the fact that they were our good southern neighbours did not give them any right to destroy our lakes, rivers, forests and fauna, and that they had no right to threaten the health of Canadians. I should not have to remind the House of the reports received by the Committee on Acid Rain which state that, each year,
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
about 15,000 people in Canada die because of acid rain, toxic emissions, holes in the ozone layer, and so on.
1 see that my time has expired, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his questions as well as the Members opposite, and I encourage all Members of this House to give very quick passage to Bill C-74. It is one of the tools that our young people need to protect their future.

Mr. Speaker, the proposed law, of course, will deal with toxic substances or a certain number of them and ensure, we hope, as it is enforced, that they do not come into Canada and are not manufactured here. We know that there are many toxic substances already here in the Great Lakes system at the bottom of the rivers and lakes and so forth. What does this Bill do, if anything, to get rid of the enormous accumulation of toxic substances already in place, particularly in our rivers and lakes?

Mr. Speaker, I see that the New Democratic Member who has been here for a number of years is asking the same questions as his colleague from Montreal was this morning, the latter however being a Liberal.
I would like to remind him that this is the first time a Government has the courage to table a bill. And it deals both with existing toxic materials and others that will be produced in the future. I am asked what we are doing about what is already under water, on river beds. I must tell you that quite a number of scientists have quite different opinions as to whether we should go down to the river beds and, by means of a siphoning process or whatever technique, remove the substances that have collected on those river beds, or whether we should simply leave them there. I must tell you that this debate is not over yet, and you may rest assured that we will continue, and the Government will continue performing the analyses and studies required before reaching the proper decision at the proper time in order to correct the errors made in years past.
If we must remove what is at the bottom of rivers, at the bottom of lakes, we will do so, although we must know whether, when stirring up the sediments at the bottom of those rivers, we will not multiply by 10, 20, or 30 the level of pollution and whether we will not be accelerating problems rather than trying to find a long-term solution.
I therefore feel this legislation is aimed at preventing what is being done as of now. But as to what was done in the past, I think we still need to have much more accurate analyses in order to develop the right technology and the right technique. And you may rest assured that the minute we know exactly what is the best means of bringing back to the environment its former quality, this Government will need no prompting, especially from the Opposition. We will on our own assume our responsibilities and will be the first to table in this House a legislation with the relevant funding, in order to be in a

September 17, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
position to give back to our youth, our future children the opportunity to enjoy a quality environment.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have mixed feelings about rising today to debate Bill C-74 which essentially proposes the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. It should be renamed because it is a minute step towards development of an environmental protection Act.
It is fair to say that we feel encouraged to support this legislation at this stage when we are discussing the principle of the Bill. However, it falls far short of the goals laid out in the first part. It sounds great when you read that first part, but as you go through it to determine what it actually accomplishes, that is unfortunately not much. I would not say it does not accomplish anything, but it is only a minute step in the right direction. We are thankful for at least that, but we have a long way to go.
I remember that for years and years in this House, particularly when the Liberal Government was in office, we called for a major initiative by the federal Government to develop a comprehensive environmental protection Act. All of us as responsible citizens recognize that without an environment which is clean, pristine, safe and healthy, we have nothing. We have been reminded just in the last few days about the dangers involved in the gradual disappearance of the ozone layer surrounding the earth and what that can do to the ecology and to people.
We spend hours and hours debating all sorts of things in this House. Some are more interesting than others. Some are more useful than others. Yet on critical issues affecting the environment, I notice that the only time it is debated is on opposition days. The Government has never introduced something which would give us an opportunity to discuss the state of the environment in Canada. That is a tragedy. That has been the case under the Conservative Government and that was the case for years and years under Liberal Governments. It is time we changed that and gave priority to our environment. We should place it before all other matters requiring consideration. If we do not preserve our pristine environment as we know it in most parts of Canada, we will have nothing in the long run. We owe it not only to our citizens today; what is more important, we owe it to our children and their children and generations yet to come.
Having said that by way of introduction, I want to point out that this Bill comes along at a time when Canadians generally are not encouraged by this Government's commitment to serious environmental protection. One of the most popular environmental issues across this country is that of leaded and unleaded gasoline. Most Canadians buy gasoline every few days. When you go to the pumps you have a choice between the two. Yet when the Government has had the opportunity to change the tax regime to encourage Canadians to use one over
the other, what do we do? We take steps to encourage them to use more leaded gasoline because it is cheaper. People see their purchasing power erode year after year and have to cut corners, and we encourage them through our tax system to purchase the worst kind of gasoline, the high lead content kind. That sends a very clear signal that the Government is not particularly concerned about lead in our environment.
I could talk about lead in other substances on which no action has been taken. I could talk about the fact that one of the major initiatives by the Government when it took office was to cut the plan to develop a Canadian toxicology centre. If we require anything, it is a centre doing research into toxic chemicals. Cutting the funding for that centre does not send a clear signal that the Government is concerned about the environment, past, present or future.
I could go on and talk about major cuts to the Canadian Wildlife Service. Many ecological and environmental activities had to be cut as a result. I could talk about the inaction of the Government on the St. Clair River blob, that great big gob of chemicals sitting in the river. Year after year we poke away at it and so on, but nothing much ever happens.
I could go on and on but I think the point is clear. Our track record in dealing effectively with environmental issues facing Canadians, indeed all people around the world, has been anything but good.
That is not to say the Government has not done anything. It would be inappropriate to say that. Yet when you look at what we should be doing, you will find that we are falling far short.
A major concern for those in the environmental movement has been the commitment of the Government to deregulation. It makes some of us sick to think, as we stand here today, that hundreds of thousands of gallons of untreated sewage is being dumped into the St. Lawrence River. The same is true of the Fraser River and others across this country. Nothing much is being done about it. We have had proposals from municipalities to deal with this critical issue which will only grow worse in the future.
The proposals involve not only cleaning up the environment but also providing thousands of jobs. They suggested a sharing arrangement such as we have had in the past where provincial Governments pay one-third, municipal Governments pay one-third, and the federal Government pays one-third to develop the necessary sewage treatment facilities. The cities were in unanimous agreement. Then the provinces all came onside. There was only one group which held out and said it was not prepared to co-operate: The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the present federal Government. That is a missed opportunity if ever there was one.
You would have to look long and hard to find a single country that does not have a program where the three levels of Government, sometimes four, share in funding of municipal infrastructure. Yet in Canada we stand alone. The federal Government says that this is not our responsibility. We will
September 17, 1987

stand by and watch the rivers die from pollution because the local tax base is simply inadequate to provide funding. Yet we have done it in the past. The federal Government used to participate in these plans. As an alderman in Kamloops I would submit proposals along with my colleagues, and they were granted, one after the other, to upgrade sewage treatment plants. However, deregulation and an unwillingness to cooperate have caused major concern and sent a negative image across the country with respect to this Government's commitment to cleaning up the environment and protecting it in the future.
I guess it was brought home to me this past summer just how critical it is to develop a federal environmental protection Act. I was out sailing in the Gulf Islands of British Columbia. As someone who travels a great deal across Canada you have probably been there and know about the pristine environment I talk about in the Gulf Islands. Clean beaches, unpolluted, no smoke-stacks, beautiful trees. A fantastically beautiful environment. I remember getting up one morning and there were about 50 pleasure craft, some very large and some very modest, in a small cove. They had lain there overnight. 1 was going to jump in and have an invigorating swim in the Pacific Ocean. I got to the side of the boat and was about to dive in when I looked at the water. The surface was covered with small pieces of thin paper and chunks of human excrement, along with all kinds of other things. People on these boats were going to the bathroom in the morning and dumping it all overboard. It was floating around all over the place. It almost made me sick. That the laws of our country, provincial, federal, or regional in this case, allow this to happen is absolutely unacceptable. This is a rather horrible description of the need for legislators at the various levels to take action immediately.
Every day when I am in Vancouver I see big barges loaded with garbage going out to dump it beyond visual limits. I shudder to think of what is going on on the ocean floor with the hundreds of thousands of tons of garbage being dumped there.
I do not want to go on about the obvious need for a decent environmental protection Act. I am sorry that this is not it. This legislation falls far short of that, but it is a step forward. I will talk about the little baby step which this legislation does take. It does take a step forward in dealing with toxic substances, because the burden of proof will lie with the company importing new toxic substances as opposed to lying with the federal Government. Until recently the federal Government had to prove that a particular industrial chemical was bad. The onus of proof will now lie on the manufacturer, and that is a step forward.
However, what about the over 60,000 industrial chemicals already in this country? I assume that some of these substances are toxic and not good for us. I believe there are 19 people in the office which looks after this. If 19 people are to
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
evaluate in excess of 60,000 chemicals, it may take centuries. In the meantime, this list is being added to by in excess of 1,000 new chemicals every year. We are faced with serious problems.
Anyone who has tried to figure out who is responsible for environmental protection knows what an incredibly tangled web there is of contradictory jurisdictional regulations. In the Department of the Environment alone there are 57 different laws dealing with environmental issues. There are 24 federal Departments dealing with environmental responsibilities. The assumption was that an intelligent government bringing forward a federal Environmental Protection Act would consolidate these.
However, nothing is done to consolidate those 24 different federal Departments. The 57 laws were reduced to 55. That is not much of a gain. People who understand what a federal environmental protection Act should be are perplexed when they learn that this tangled web will remain.
There is, of course, a dispute over who is responsible. For three years I have been working with the Shuswap Concerned Citizens Committee. You will be aware, Mr. Speaker, that there are hundreds of house boats which float on the large Shuswap Lake complex in central British Columbia. All sorts of things enter the water from these boats. This is a large lake, but when the people on hundreds of house boats and thousands of pleasure craft dump things into the water a serious problem develops.
The various jurisdictions have been trying to determine who is responsible for ensuring that this water remains clean. Is it the local regional district? Is it the various provincial departments? Are federal Departments involved and, if so, which Departments? For three years I have been trying to figure that out and still have not been able to determine who is responsible because no one accepts responsibility. Due to the overlapping jurisdictional regions we find a great deal of buck-passing going on.
I want to read from a report by the Canadian Environmental Law Association to the Special Joint Committee on the Constitutional Accord. It says:
The Constitution Act, 1987, which reflected the problems and concerns of 1867 when it was enacted, did not allocate legislative authority for the environment to either the federal or provincial governments. As a result, there is a large degree of overlapping jurisdiction because of the generality of the federal and provincial powers as defined in the Constitution. Without clear responsibility for environmental concerns, both levels of government have been able to disclaim authority for dealing with environmental problems by alleging that it is within the other's jurisdiction. This has resulted in "jurisdictional buck-passing."
Such is the case, Mr. Speaker. It is now time for the federal Government to exert a strong federal presence to deal with environmental problems which are national in scope. The Canadian Environmental Law Association said further:
We have also maintained that the federal government has the clear constitutional authority to take action in regard to many of the environmental

September 17, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
problems of the 1980s. This is especially the case in the area of toxic
chemicals, which do not respect provincial boundaries.
They go on to point out that this situation, bad at the moment, could get even worse in the future as a result of the Meech Lake Accord.
The solution to this problem is obvious. It requires a federal government which has the will and commitment to deal effectively with environmental issues. I suspect that if we were to take on that responsibility, our provincial colleagues would be quite pleased to agree that this is a federal responsibility and would allow us to get on with dealing with it to ensure that our land, water, and air remain clean or are cleaned up.
As Canadians become more and more involved with pleasure crafts on the waters of Canada, particularly the inland waters, the matter of gray water becomes more of a problem. Gray water is dishwater, shower water, or soapy water as opposed to black water which contains human excrement. At the moment there is absolutely no restriction on gray water in the Shuswap area and only vague restrictions on black water. Slowly but surely the entire Shuswap Lake system is being polluted. Once we reach a point of no return the lake will be finished, as has already happened to some waters in central Canada.
My friend, the Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), was pointing out to this House how odd it is to see in the summer, in the great City of Toronto, people on the beaches lining up to swim in the swimming pools because the water at the shoreline is polluted. That is a tragedy which we must take action collectively to change.
1 also want to comment on PCBs. It has been brought to my attention that PCBs are entering the underground water system in parts of Canada. Many submersible pumps, particularly those imported from the United States, have PCBs in their insulation and wiring. These pumps are lowered into wells where they operate near the groundwater level. They are often abandoned as they break down or properties are sold. These pumps then deteriorate and PCBs leak into the water system.
There is only way for people buying these properties to determine whether there are PCBs in the water and that is to give the pump to Environment Canada which will analyse the pump by destroying it. It is not an encouragement for people to have such an analysis done to know that Environment Canada will destroy their S3,000 pump in order to tell them whether or not there are PCBs in the water. There must be a greater commitment to deal with PCBs in the underground water system by establishing a decent investigation process to determine whether or not these elements are in our water supply.
The whole area of pesticides has been left out of this legislation. A great deal of work must be done in this area, and I do not believe anyone would suggest that the federal Government does not have a responsibility to deal with this.
One of the greatest shortcomings of Bill C-74 is that it does not include an environmental Bill of rights. Environmentalists and others who are concerned about the environment for many reasons strongly believe that there is a need for a Bill of environmental rights and the ability to resort to the courts to ensure that our environment is preserved in a clean and pristine nature.
Considering the absence of a Bill of environmental rights, which we feel is an absolute necessity, the fact that major sectors have been ignored, and the fact that the Bill does nothing to consolidate this vast web of interlocking jurisdictions and regulations, we will be offering amendments at the legislative committee stage in order to improve the Bill.
The best we can do at this stage is to pass the Bill quickly, realizing that it is a small step toward an Environmental Protection Act. We can begin from scratch again and, with proper consultation this time, bring forward a Bill that does represent what an Environmental protection Act ought to represent.

As always, I listened with interest to the Hon. Member's comments. I feel compelled to respond to each comment, but time will not permit me to do so. However, let me attempt to respond quickly to a few of his points.
First, he expressed great concern about the lack of time made available in this Parliament to debate environmental matters. In fact, one year ago, the issue of environmental protection was very much an integral and significant part of the Speech from the Throne. The Government provided some eight days after the Speech from the Throne in which the Hon. Member, any of his colleagues, or anyone in the House, could have debated matters of environmental affairs if they wished to do so. While I have not looked at the record, I suspect that there was very little time devoted by the Hon. Member and his colleagues to the question of environmental affairs during that debate on the Speech from the Throne.
The Hon. Member repeated a comment which had been made in the House on a number of occasions yesterday and today by opposition Members, that is, that the Government has done virtually nothing with respect to the environment in the past three years. The Member knows that that is certainly far from the truth. The Government has taken many actions in that respect. This includes action on acid rain, with a national program to reduce acid rain by 50 per cent of its 1980 levels by 1994. They include a commitment to spend SI50 million for emission controls at smelters, $25 million for technology development, $70 million for cleaner use of coal, and $18 million per year in research and monitoring.
There is a commitment to increase the use of western low-sulphur coal. The Hon. Member knows that great strides have been made in negotiations between the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) and the Premier of the Province of Ontario with respect to the use by Ontario Hydro of low-sulphur western coal.
September 17, 1987

On September 1, new automobile emission standards to reduce acid rain were introduced. In addition, there was an agreement between the federal Government, the Province of Ontario, the Government of the United States and the Government of New York State with respect to reducing the flow of toxic chemicals from the dumps along the Niagara River into the Niagara River and Lake Ontario. Furthermore, there has been the tightening up of standards with respect to the transportation of dangerous goods by rail.
Just within the last day or so we saw the international ozone treaty.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member. Could he put his question, please?
Mr. Red way: Mr. Speaker, I have had a chance only to mention a few things.
However, there is one matter that really bothered me. The Hon. Member indicated that he, as a councillor in the City of Kamloops, was able to obtain federal funding on numerous occasions for the reduction of pollution as far as water treatment and sewage were concerned. That interested me specifically because I know that in my municipality, in spite of years and years of trying, the only time we were able to get any federal money was when the former Government was so desperate to get re-elected in the last years of its mandate that it went around making special grants to very selected municipalities, including ours. Will the Hon. Member give me some examples of the federal Government in the past sharing these projects? I would like to have the opportunity to make that case with the Government.

Mr. Speaker, it would be my pleasure to answer the last question first. In 1968 or 1969, the Liberal federal Government at the time offered to enter into an agreement on a cost-sharing formula with provincial Governments. The federal Government made an offer to enter into an agreement with the Government of British Columbia which, in turn, entered into an agreement with the municipalities, according to the constitutional jurisdictions of the country.
The critical factor was an agreement first being made between the federal and provincial Governments. I believe the Conservative Government in Ontario at the time was unwilling to participate in that program, so that perhaps it never existed in the Province of Ontario. However, it did exist in Alberta, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia.
The provincial Governments signed separate agreements with the federal Government and then signed separate agreements with the various municipalities to participate in a three-way cost-sharing for a municipal infrastructure, not only for sewage treatment facilities, but for water upgrading facilities generally and roads, sidewalks, lights and so on. Obviously, the Ontario Conservative Government at the time did not want to participate.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
At the outset, I said that the fact that issues of environmental concern were only debated when the Opposition chose to do so was an indication of the federal Government's commitment to environmental concerns. My hon. friend said there were opportunities to debate this during the Throne Speech. I was waiting for him to indicate other occasions on which this has been debated because we are required to debate countless issues that are included in a Throne Speech. Rather than an environmental debate, it is a Throne Speech debate. However, the Hon. Member did not mention any other occasions on which environmental issues were debated. It is a pathetic state of affairs when the only argument the Hon. Member can make is to say that we had a Throne Speech debate a year and a half ago.
Finally, in the fourth year of the administration, we welcome the opportunity to begin a debate on this matter of environmental protection.
The Hon. Member mentioned western coal as one of the initiatives of the Government. In all fairness, I believe I said that the Government has taken some initiatives. Incidentally, this initiative was introduced by one of my New Democratic Party colleagues from the Kootenay area in British Columbia in 1981. At that time, we felt that this was an appropriate initiative to take and began the process.
It is interesting that the Hon. Member raised this question because the head of the miners' union for that area is in the lobby listening to the debate right now. He just happens to be here at this time. He also worked with the NDP Member from the Kootenays at the time to begin this process moving with the previous administration and the Ontario Government. I am pleased to say we are still moving. Perhaps sometime in the next little while we will have an agreement. However, I do know that the report which was done by the special task force looking into this matter made not a single recommendation for further study, further deliberations and so on. Again, if the Government meant what it says it means, it would take action, not study, study, study.
Here is a situation where we can improve the acid rain phenomenon in central Canada, we can provide the much needed jobs in both central and western Canada. Let us get on with it. What are we waiting for?
This proposal was introduced by my colleague from the Kootenay region of British Columbia in 1981, and we are pleased that we are debating this again today. But let us recognize that we have a long way to go. What is required is a federal Government with a will and commitment to deal with these difficult and major issues. Quite frankly, we do not have any alternative. We must deal with these issues.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member quoted from a letter from the Canadian Environmental Law Association, the Citizens' Network on Waste Management, Pollution Probe and Energy Probe, who are concerned that the Meech Lake

September 17, 1987
Adjournment Motion
Agreement and, in particular, the right of the provinces to opt out of shared-cost programs, may discourage the federal Government from assuming its responsibility to protect the nation's environment. They are particularly concerned that the uncertainty created by the ambiguous nature of Section 106 relating to shared-cost programs, may affect such potential shared-cost programs as setting up a super fund to clean up toxic waste dump sites.
The letter is addressed to the Special Joint Committee on the 1987 Constitutional Accord. It is dated September 10 of this year. I believe the committee wrapped up its work by September 10 and the report was to be published last week. However, it has been delayed because of translation problems. In the concluding paragraph of the letter they urge the committee to proceed with caution and to consider substantive revisions to the sections relating to shared-cost programs to clarify that the Accord does not take away from the federal Government's authority to set national standards for environmental protection.
I would like to ask the Member, first, if he shares those concerns. He quoted from the letter, so I presume he shares those concerns, but I would like him to state so specifically, if that is indeed the case. Second, I would like to know what he and his Party are prepared to do about it. Will his Party be proposing an amendment to the Meech Lake Accord in that respect? I would be very pleased to hear his views in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, first, I think the point made by my hon. friend when he quoted from the letter of the Canadian Environmental Law Association is accurate. It is concerned that Section 106(a)(2), which states that the section does not alter the existing division of powers, again does not help us in defining what is exclusive provincial jurisdiction in environmental matters. In terms of the point the Hon. Member makes regarding the national shared-cost programs in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction, I think it has been demonstrated by the work of the committee. I recall reading a transcript of the proceedings which indicated that this matter was dealt with, and in fact national cost-shared programs may even be enhanced, so that it was decided by the all-Party committee that it was not of critical concern.
However, 1 do not think that this is the issue here. I think the issue is that even if it were-which of course it is-a concern, if the federal Government took the initiative and said: "We are not going to turn Canada into a toxic waste dump for North America or wherever", and made that commitment and then put into place a federal program to provide that special fund to provide for the clean-up of existing hazardous waste sites and abandoned and enclosed waste sites, it would develop a sense in our country that this is something that must be done. If the Government said this is something that must be done and something we are prepared to fund, any province daring to opt out of that program, or any province that would dare not to implement its own program of even increased standards, would
be severely condemned by the electorate in that province or territory.
I think the concern is a serious one. It has been one of concern to my caucus. During the deliberations, on balance, we felt that it is a concern that was simply flagged, but in reality that is not the case. Even if it were, it is the will of this Parliament and the will of this Government combined that would ensure that such would not take place, and the concerns that were brought to the joint committee's attention by the Canadian Environmental Law Association, if we do our job properly, would never have to be a concern.

The House resumed considertion of the motion of Mr. McMillan that Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure this afternoon to have the opportunity to speak on this legislation, something about which all Canadians are concerned.
I would like to say that this Bill, on which the Minister has done considerable work, will receive support right across the country. The legislation introduced by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) will unquestionably make Canada a leader in the battle to prevent pollution from toxic
September 17, 1987

chemicals and thereby protect the public from adverse health effects which could result from exposure to such pollution.
Protecting the environment is not the sole responsibility of any one Department, one Government, one province, or even one nation. Toxic chemical pollution is a world-wide problem and demands intra-national as well as international cooperation to achieve solutions.
There is another more obvious reason, however, why this is a joint effort. This legislation is intended not only to protect our environment for its own sake, but also to protect the environment because of its direct link with human health.
It has been realized for some time that there are numerous opportunities for the wide variety of complex chemical products in use in Canada today to be released into the environment during manufacture, use, transportation and eventual disposal. These releases can result in contamination of the food, air and drinking water on which humans depend for their well-being and, indeed, survival. Exposure to environmental contaminants can have serious effects on health and longterm social and economic consequences.
The primary concern of the Department of Health and Welfare is the threat posed to the health and well-being of the Canadian population by either short-term or long-term exposure to the environmental contaminants, which are often present at relatively low levels. Of particular concern is the prospect that health effects may only be observed after long periods of exposure or long after exposure has ceased to occur.
Chemicals can bestow enormous benefits on mankind, but we must ensure that our health is not compromised in the process. This is a major thrust in this legislation. This Bill will provide the necessary power to move much further than before in developing objectives and guidelines for environmental quality that are designed to ensure that our environment remains in a healthful condition.
There are several factors which contribute to the complexity of toxic chemical problems. The number of chemicals in use is very large and is constantly increasing. Individual chemicals are complex in nature. There are numerous sources and mechanisms for release of chemicals to the environment. The Canadian population is being exposed to a complex mixture of chemicals, and the effects of exposure are difficult to estimate. Some chemicals that are likely to have minimal impact on the health of most Canadians may have great impact on the health of groups within the general population who, for reasons of age, sex or genetic composition, economic status, occupation, lifestyle or geographical location are more sensitive to the effects of certain toxic chemicals.
My concern, and of course the concern of all Canadians, is over health hazards associated with chemicals in the environment, which can well be illustrated by examples such as the contamination of edible fish with mercury compounds that
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
leaked from plants formerly used to produce chlorine and alkali used in the manufacture of pulp and paper. It was the consumption of fish tainted with mercury in this way that placed the residents of Grassy Narrows in northwestern Ontario at risk.
Another widely dispersed metal which poses a threat to human health is lead. The toxic effects of lead are well known. The major source of lead in our environment is the burning of leaded gasoline in motor vehicles. While measures have been taken to reduce exposure to lead by phasing out the use of leaded gasolines and, indeed, to reduce exposure from other sources of lead in the environment, we must remain vigilant and reassure ourselves that substitute products are safe both from an environmental and health viewpoint.
I am sure that all of us are aware of the threats posed by synthetic organic chemicals such as PCBs which, by virtue of their resistance to degradation, can persist and accumulate in living organisms. From a health standpoint PCBs are not extremely toxic in terms of short-term exposure. Long-term exposure is of concern because of the effects on the liver, reproduction, the immune system and the possibility that PCBs, or impurities contained in them, may be associated with cancer.
Over the years the federal Government has enacted several laws to combat the effects of toxic chemicals. Control of toxic substances is required from manufacture to disposal. Legislative control, federal and provincial, must cover the following elements: manufacture, importation, transportation, storage and handling, use and sale, discharge to water, air and land, spills, occupational health, and ultimate disposal.
There are some 24 federal statutes which exercise some form of control respecting toxic substances. For example, the basic regulations for contaminants in food and drug products are found in regulations under the Food and Drugs Act.
The Fisheries Act prohibits the deposition of a "deleterious substance" of any type in water frequented by fish. The Hazardous Products Act is a product-oriented statute which prohibits the advertisement, sale and information of certain hazardous products, and which was recently amended to ensure that workers are given information relating to workplace hazardous products.
The Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act has been designed to promote public safety in the transportation of dangerous goods, including chemicals. The Ocean Dumping Control Act is designed to control dumping of waste and other substances into the ocean.
Notwithstanding the scope of these various statutes, the proposed Canadian Environmental Protection Act provides a focused and integrated approach to toxic chemicals. It will allow the federal Government, in co-operation with the provinces, industry, labour, and the public, to identify different ways to reduce human exposure to chemicals at each stage of their life cycle. The control of toxic chemicals as envisaged in

September 17, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
this Bill was not possible under the provisions of the Environmental Contaminants Act, the Clean Air Act, and the parts of the Canada Water Act which are now incorporated into this proposed legislation.
The public is deeply concerned about what is sometimes viewed as a fragmented approach to dealing with chemicals. Our laws do not meet public expectations. Often, they are products of dealing with the problems of past decades. They are inadequate for dealing with the problems of today. They must be revamped, streamlined, consolidated, and they must address the real problems of environmental protection.
I believe that Canadians need and deserve a comprehensive management approach for toxic chemicals, an approach that manages chemicals throughout their life cycle in a manner that prevents them from leaking into the environment. It will mean that at any stage in the life of a chemical from cradle to grave-whether it is its introduction into trade and commerce, its manufacturing, its transportation, its use or disposal-all participants who use and care for that chemical must act in a responsible manner to protect the environment and the health of Canadians.
When consumers such as ourselves use chemicals, we must be equipped with the best information to use them properly, to dispose of them safely, to act in an emergency situation, and to choose alternative products and practices.
Chemicals must be transported and stored in a manner that eliminates leakage to the environment. If accidents do happen, clean-up must be fast and effective and victims must be compensated in a just and equitable fashion.
We must not forget disposal, both for the chemical itself after its useful life and for wastes. Waste cannot continue to be added to the environment in the naive hope that the environment can safely accommodate it and cleanse itself. We can no longer say that the solution to pollution is dilution. There must be adequate destruction facilities operating in this country to dispose of hazardous waste.
In particular, I am encouraged by the process whereby the legislation that is before us today has been developed. All affected segments of society, including representatives of industry, workers and environmental interest groups alike, have taken part in developing a scheme that relies upon good scientific knowledge to develop the regulations that will underpin this legislation. The result of this is agreement by all parties concerned on the need for adequate testing of chemicals, and a basic understanding of the way in which the knowledge that emerges can be most effectively used to prevent injury, disease and death from accidents and pollution problems.
The sheer number of chemicals we use is intimidating. Over 65,000 are produced commercially on the global market with over 1,000 new ones added annually. Only a small fraction have been tested for the environmental and health consequences. We must clearly define the ground rules for allowing
a chemical to enter the Canadian market. Since we are part of the global chemical market, we are promoting the adoption and utilization of common international approaches to evaluating chemicals and to setting standards. We must also promote alternatives to the use of high-risk chemicals.
Canada alone cannot test all the chemicals we use in a reasonable timeframe. It has to be an international effort. It is one we are committed to put in place and we are working hard through the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development and the International Program of Chemical Safety to do just that. There is a lack of public confidence in the country when it comes to chemical management. Our ability to solve the problems has not kept pace with our ability to detect the problems.
The proposed Canadian Environmental Protection Act represents a crucial step in developing a comprehensive strategy to control toxic chemicals in the environment. The extensive consultation which followed the introduction in Parliament in December, 1986, of the proposed environmental protection Act, has indeed been invaluable in helping to attain this objective. As a result of these consultations and submission of numerous briefs, the legislation now proposed has been broadened to incorporate the provisions of the Ocean Dumping Control Act; increase the emphasis on evaluating and controlling existing chemicals; include provisions to deal with the products of biotechnology; require the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) to develop guidelines, objectives, and codes of practice to protect health and the environment; provide for enhanced public participation in implementing provisions of the Act; and provide for working cooperatively with provincial Governments to avoid duplication and overlap.
We have already mentioned the value of developing an environmental protection strategy that allows for the control of toxic chemicals from the time that they are introduced into commerce until their ultimate disposal.
One of the key factors of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act is that it focuses on preventing the introduction into commerce of chemicals that will constitute a danger to public health or the environment. For example, the "new chemicals" provisions of this legislation will place the onus on industry to demonstrate the safety of new chemicals prior to their use in Canada.
The new Canadian Environmental Protection Act puts human health and safety where it should be, before everything else. Under the new life cycle management approach, decisions affecting human health will be incorporated into the decisionmaking process. They will no longer be relegated to the realm of afterthoughts.
In addition, the new Act will extend the Government's authority to set national environmental standards, guidelines,
September 17, 1987

and objectives. These guidelines presently exist for the emission of toxic substances into the atmosphere and would be retained in the new Act. The new Act would be expanded to include water and land, using the Clean Air Act as a model.
The new national standards would be developed in cooperation with provincial Governments. They could be used by provinces and municipalities as the basis for regulations to provide minimum levels of environmental quality across the country.
The Canadian Environmental Protection Act will also help Canada meets its international obligations with such bodies as the United Nations Environment Program, and the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development.
Under the new legislation, exporters who intend to ship toxic chemicals to a foreign country would be required to inform the country of that intention. We will benefit in Canada because participating countries will extend the same courtesy to us. This will allow us to better prepare for and control the amount of toxic chemicals that come into Canada, and thus better protect human life.
I wish to conclude by saying that ultimately our society will have to come to grips with the fact that many of our environmental problems are rooted in the lifestyles that we have chosen. We have chosen a chemical society, and with it, the responsibility to protect our life support system from our dependence on these chemicals.
I believe that Canadians are ready to take a major step toward learning to live successfully and respectfully with chemicals. The Canadian Environmental Protection Act represents a major contribution to this endeavour.

I wish to ask my hon. colleague a question since he represents the government side of the House. I am glad to see that a senior Minister from British Columbia is also present, and I am sure she is interested.
Does the Hon. Member think that the federal Government has a responsibility to ensure that government agencies do not contribute to environmental pollution?
I wish to give an example. In Vancouver East, the Port of Vancouver which is a federal jurisdiction contains a large garbage incinerator on a barge that is moored very close to a residential neighbourhood. This barge is the method by which all the garbage is burned from the cruise ships in the Port of Vancouver. It emits a foul smell and smoke which pollutes the neighbourhood for many blocks.
Since this is a federal jurisdiction, the Port Corporation for Vancouver is a federal agency, and the manager of the Port Corporation refuses to take any action. I wonder what are the views of the Hon. Member. Does he think that the federal Government should intervene? If so, what action can be taken?
Canadian Environmental Protection Act

First, I wish to say to the Hon. Member that I believe both the federal Government and the federal Crown corporation should be involved. The legislation that we have put forward today gives an opportunity to those involved. I would say that in the Hon. Member's riding, representation should be made under the new guidelines, and certainly it should be looked at.

The Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall) has raised a number of sensible points in his speech. I wish to ask the Hon. Member a specific question which perplexes us. The preamble to Bill C-74 is very specific on the federal responsibility for environmental pollution. It refers to the environment as a matter of national concern; toxic substances once introduced into the environment cannot always be contained within geographical boundaries, particularly provincial boundaries. The Government of Canada in demonstrating national leadership should establish national environmental quality objectives, guidelines and practices. It refers to Canadian waters and other federal responsibilities.
Yet Members on the government side have used constitutional excuses for government inaction. One Hon. Member even stated that the Charter of Rights was an excuse for the federal Government not to take action on environmental protection. It is an absolutely astounding idea that we should be gaining civil rights but losing the power to protect the environment. I think that is quite an astonishing development.
I wish to ask the Hon. Member how he can justify the statement of national priority concern and responsibility with the cop-out on the part of the federal Government, and the willingness to leave it up to the provinces. If they do not legislate adequately, tough luck, use the constitutional excuse that the federal Government has not been given the specific power to act in this area and somehow it does not have a responsibility to act for our environmental protection.
