In a short period of time this Government has taken many steps in many directions to attempt to make a better way for all Canadians. The Bill before us indicates that the Government and this Minister are prepared to sit down with both the provinces and the industry in order to start to work together to solve some of these real problems.
These problems did not happen today. They have developed over the last many years. It is with this type of legislation and this Government that we will be able to sit down and negotiate with the provinces and the industries to make sure that there is a happy medium. Those individuals who may be involved within an industry will still have the opportunity to have the employment that is required, and the provinces will be able to adapt to the guidelines within this legislation.

The Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall) has ably set out the factors involved in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. He has touched on the aspect of a number of chemicals in the environment, and touched a raw nerve with me. I am very concerned about the

September 17, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
fact that chemicals are there. We do not know what they are presently doing, or what they will do in the future. Will the Hon. Member comment further on the manner in which the new Canadian Environmental Protection Act will deal with chemicals that are already in use?

We are aware that someone who comes from a northern region, or other parts of the country, has great concerns. What we should look to is that the Minister of the Environment place an increased emphasis on screening the chemicals to ensure that the products are ones that we feel comfortable with, ones that perhaps we are looking at coming in, and that they be screened before Canadians make use of them. This is one part of the Bill with which I feel very comfortable. We will be screening those chemicals which are coming in and those chemicals which are here now to make certain that the environment is looked after properly.

Mr. Speaker, I have two questions for the Hon. Member. First, he talked about consultation on the part of the Government, provincial Governments, and organizations interested in the environment. He left the impression that the Bill, as a result of consultations, meets the objections, questions, and criticisms of past practices made by many of these organizations.
is the Hon. Member aware of the fact that the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian Environmental Law Association, two major organizations, are very critical of the Bill because so much of what needs to be done is not covered in it?
I have another question for the Hon. Member because he represents part of northern Ontario in which there are a number of mines and a number of pulp and paper mills, two industries that have been notorious for their ability to maximize their profits by dumping waste products into our rivers and lakes.
Is there anything in this Bill, or in any other Bill, which gives Canadians any confidence that in the next 10 years or 15 years such irresponsible activity will cease to continue?

Mr. Speaker, the introduction of this Bill is certainly a step forward which has not been taken by any previous Government. I think that is the first thing we must recognize.
I am interested in some of the items about which the Hon. Member talked, such as the Canadian Labour Congress. We have come quite a distance in bringing forth this piece of legislation.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government always believe in going out to speak with Canadians, whether in provincial Government, labour, or business, to ensure that they know the thoughts of Canadians before moving forward. The Hon. Member must realize that the Canadian Labour
Congress certainly has its views, but we are taking a step which is very positive for the environment.
The Hon. Member referred to mines and paper mills in northern Ontario. There has been quite a change in the last three years to five years with regard to upgrading and in terms of pollution going into our waters. Filtration plants in the mills have been changed.
With regard to mines, I think the industry itself has recognized that changes were required. However, on the other hand, I ask the Hon. Member how far we can go and be able to compete in the international market with other countries.
Would he sooner see individuals in the mines and pulp and paper industries not having jobs, or would he sooner see the Government and the provinces working toward a goal to clean up the environment as best we can yet still be competitive in the international market?

First, Mr. Speaker, I should like to pay tribute to the non-governmental organizations which are dedicated to protecting our environment. Mr. Speaker, you are certainly aware that hundreds of organizations from coast to coast play a fundamental role in educating and motivating the public, as well as in lobbying the Government and parliamentarians. All these efforts contribute to creating a public opinion which is highly receptive and fully aware of the need to protect the environment. 1 feel confident that you agree with me that an enlightened public opinion is prerequisite to any government action.
Canadians often ask themselves the question: What can I do? This question has often been put to me, by younger people particularly. The answer is simple. Get involved in nongovernmental organizations like the Greenpeace Foundation whose Montreal regional office is located in my own riding of Laurier, or the Canadian Wildlife Federation, Pollution Probe, hundreds of suchlike organizations which are active throughout this country. The impact and benefits of this kind of commitment cannot be understated.
When the World Commission on Environment released their report last spring the Canadian representative, Mr. Maurice Strong, came here to Ottawa to meet with parliamentarians and spokesmen for organizations actively working in the environment and wildlife sector. Sad to say, only two or three Members attended this meeting.
What struck me most in the message conveyed by the World Commission on Environment is that we must divorce ourselves from segmentation in our approach to environmental issues. Environmental problems cannot be tackled on an isolated basis. For example, hydro power plants produce electricity in many regions, but other people are made responsible for eliminating the resulting acid rains.
Mr. Speaker, the challenge facing us today is twofold: first, making economic development agencies-and even the
September 17, 1987

Minister of Finance-responsible for that sector of the environment which is affected by their decisions; and, second, environment ministries in the various countries must wield more power to fight pollution.

The sense I got from the report of the World Commission on Environment and Development was that the most difficult challenge we are facing is to develop management systems on national and international levels to deal with environmental and developmental problems which defy simple, compartmentalized ways of looking at things.
This is the standard against which we must measure the Bill we are studying today. Is it forward looking? Is it innovative? Will it provide the means to come to grips with urgent environmental problems posed by economic development?
It is also particularly important to remember that environmental legislation in Canada is reviewed only once every 10 years or so. We must use the opportunity before us at the present time to get it right. This point was made by Toby Vigod of the Canadian Environmental Law Association.
While Bill C-74 establishes procedures to deal with new chemicals, it is not particularly innovative and does not get around the institutional and management problems which have plagued us in the past. On the contrary-the Conservative Government abdicates its responsibility to set national standards and leaves environmental protection up to the provinces.
Take, for example, the idea of an environmental Bill of rights, which the Minister has in the not so distant past espoused. In fact, very recently he was an advocate of such an environmental Bill of rights. This novel approach has been abandoned in Bill C-74. What we have instead is a preamble to this Bill which is not legally enforceable. It does not confer rights on citizens to protect their environment, which is what every group has been asking for. It does not provide a right to protect the environment in cases where personal damage has not occurred. Yet as far back as 1970, other jurisdictions have given citizens the right to take polluters to court even in cases where they have not suffered direct damage.
Some of the most striking provisions of this Bill are those that would require the Minister to consult all the provinces before he or she drafts regulations or issues emergency orders to control toxic chemicals. It is laughable that even in the event of an emergency, there are stringent consultation requirements before the Minister of the Environment for Canada (Mr. McMillan) can take action. Even in the event of an emergency he is obliged to go through a painstaking consultation process. The Minister, furthermore, is allowed to regulate only if he is satisfied that not all of the provincial Governments are prepared to implement provisions, and I am quoting here "substantially the same as those contained in the regulation" which the Minister proposes to adopt. Here we
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
come to the $64,000 question. What is meant by "substantially the same"? Who will decide what is meant by that? The Minister? The provinces? The courts after extensive legal challenges? What if the provinces argue that their regulations are substantially the same, even if their standards are much lower? Will this not ensure that any national program will amount to the lowest common denominator, to which all of the provinces may agree?
Is this language not strangely reminiscent of the Meech Lake Agreement in which the federal Government has transferred enormous powers to the provinces? Does this same spirit not doom the idea of a super fund to clean up abandoned waste disposal sites? The Canadian Environmental Law Association proposed that such a fund be created through a tax on chemical feed stocks and waste disposal owners and operators. Presumably such an initiative to create a super fund to clean up toxic waste dumps would require some kind of provincial participation, even if it is limited to the road leading up to the dump. Before you can say Meech Lake, Mr. Speaker, we will have a shared-cost program. I hate to say so, but before you know it, the provinces will be able to say, "Well, we, under the Meech Lake Agreement, will set up our own program. We will opt out of the federal program". Again, it will take years of litigation before we determine whether a provincial program is substantially the same or is compatible with the objectives set out in the federal initiative, which I think reflects the language in the Meech Lake Agreement.
This concern was raised by the Canadian Environmental Law Association, the Citizens' Network on Waste Management, Pollution Probe and Energy Probe in a recent letter to the Clerk of the standing joint committee on the Constitution. They feel that the right of the provinces to opt out of shared-cost programs may discourage the federal Government from assuming its responsibility in the area of environmental protection if it can be argued that an initiative may be in an area of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. Even a program in an area of concurrent jurisdiction where both the federal and provincial Governments have jurisdiction may be affected by this provision, as was noted by the groups in their letter.
As our spokesman for the environment, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), stated yesterday, Bill C-74 should propose strong national standards that can only be superseded by provincial legislation which is stronger than federal legislation, but surely not by provincial legislation which is weaker. Instead, what we have with Bill C-74 is legislation which will ensure that the federal Government will give in to lower provincial standards and, therefore, create a chequer-board type of treatment of the environment across Canada, in other words, better protection of the environment in one province than in the other, which defies the nature of pollution which very often cuts across boundaries and artificial boundaries.
What about water, Mr. Speaker? Apart from our hockey players, I think you would agree with me that water is Canada's greatest natural resource. Yet this Bill contains no

September 17, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
provisions to establish national water quality standards and no authority to set drinking water quality standards. Furthermore, the major provisions of the federal water pollution law currently found in the Fisheries Act have not been incorporated into this Bill, and therefore some of the progressive and innovative sentencing techniques found in this Bill will not apply to those who pollute our waters. Bill C-74 does not deal with the hundreds of toxic chemicals found today in Canada's waterways.
This Bill will be referred to a legislative committee for study, Mr. Speaker. 1 hope that members of the committee take full advantage of the opportunity to improve the Bill, particularly in light of the fact that it is only once in a decade when Canada's environmental laws are revised and we get to study a Bill of this nature. I hope the Bill will be turned into the kind of forward-looking, innovative legislation that will provide the means for Canada to deal with the urgent environmental problems which face us today.

In considering what amendments should be made, the committee can do no better than to refer to the recommendations of the environmental groups of Canada which met on June 25 and focussed on three proposals for amendments.
First, that we recognize the legal right of citizens to take legal action; and included in the same recommendation, that we provide financial assistance to ordinary citizens so that they may take part in the decision-making process. As everyone knows, the companies involved in the decision-making process can deduct their expenses from their taxable income, which means that half their legal costs are paid by Canadian taxpayers. Ordinary citizens and environmental groups do not have the same financial resources as companies and should receive some financial assistance from the Government.
Second, that we reinforce the power of the Government to apply anti-pollution standards. There should be national standards, and this should not be left under the sole jurisdiction of the provinces.
Third, these groups emphasized the importance of creating a data bank to which those involved would have access and which would include the standards for the quality of life and the protection of the environment which the Government intends to apply.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by saying it is a pleasure to speak to this Bill, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health. As my colleague from Kamloops-Shuswap said, there is certainly no issue more important than this on which the time of this House should be spent.
As my colleagues have said, we are happy to see the Government introducing a first step, yet it reflects what we
have seen from all Governments historically in Canada, a form of crisis management as opposed to a strong political will to deal with this very serious issue. Because of that, we see a general lack of faith by the public in the environmental information we receive. This has very serious consequences. It means that much of the information Governments of all Parties give out may be received with less than enthusiastic acceptance. There have been many cover-ups, not necessarily by Governments or political Parties, in an attempt to avoid alarming the public over particular environmental issues. Again, the legislation is positive but it reflects an attitude of crisis management.
There are a few areas I would like to address which illustrate that. First, I would like to speak to a particular issue relative to the area I represent north of the 60th parallel. Nowhere else do we see the importance of good environmental legislation which balances the need for development and the need for preserving the environment. I happen to be one of those who believe that this is possible if the political will is there. It does not have to be a choice between jobs or the environment. We need both for our life and health, and both must be in balance. For example, I quote Don Gamble, Executive Director of the Ottawa-based Rassion Academy of Aquatic Science, speaking in Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories. He said, concerning water pollution, that:
Governments must do more than collect water data and regulate effluents.
Their efforts should be based on what is called an eco-systems approach which
recognizes that all economic activity ultimately depends on a viable
environment.
It is therefore my belief that legislation can achieve both these objectives and do it well. If we do not, the future of our economy and our health is in jeopardy.
Canada has a long history of resource extraction without proper controls. This has resulted in legal uncertainty for both the industry and those involved with the environment. North of 60 is often referred to as the last frontier. I suggest that for many people it is the last frontier environmentally as well as in other respects. It is the last chance to do things the right way. We have not totally polluted the environment and we must be particularly vigilant.
To some extent I agree that this Bill begins to address the important area of toxins. That, after all, is the major thrust of the Bill. Yet one of the things it omits is a Bill of rights for environmental health. I strongly believe that an Act presented as protecting human life and health must include that Bill of rights. The history of our country is such that medical care has been the right of all Canadian citizens. Surely environmental protection, a clean and unpolluted environment, is the concomitant Bill of rights, otherwise a medical care Bill of rights does not make much sense.
I would like to address three areas in the Bill which I think warrant greater discussion in committee. First is the question of enforcement. I have seen many instances where we have had really quite good laws on the books but neither the resources to carry out enforcement nor in some cases the will. Certainly the
September 17, 1987

Government will have to commit itself to putting forward adequate resources for enforcement. Otherwise, it again underscores the lack of faith the public has in laws and regulations, and undermines the public's faith in the bureaucracy and politicians, as well as generates a sense of hopelessness over the question of whether anything can really be done about the environment.
That is something one sees as having happened through the 1970s when there was a great environmental movement. As we move through the 1980s the problems become more complex because of new chemicals being created every day, a problem which this Bill attempts to address. Yet there is an increasing sense of hopelessness. What can we do? Therefore, legislation must ensure enforcement in order to give hope to people.
I feel that this Bill does not illustrate as strong a commitment to enforcement as we would like to see. Clause 7 says that the Minister "may" do certain things with respect to enforcement. That illustrates the point I was making earlier. There are adequate laws on the books, but they are not enforced. It is not necessarily so because people do not want to enforce them; there may not be the personnel and so on. In order to maintain the public faith and send the message that the Government is serious, the objectives outlined in Clause 7 should be made much stronger and I hope this will be given consideration when the Bill is in committee.
North of 60 we have had a number of examples of a lack of enforcement. That is why I feel so strongly about it. We have territorial water boards under the Northern Inland Waters Act. That Act is fairly adequate. However, the enforcement capability of those water boards is really not very strong and is subject to a lot of controversy involving the industries affected, involving legal certainty, as well as the public at large who ask, what is the point in having hearings, interventions and guidelines if in the end nothing can be enforced? There is no recourse for those who are concerned that such guidelines and regulations be carried out.
With regard to Clause 7, which provides that the Minister may do a number of important things which I think should be done, an issue right now which is of consequence to all of Canada, in particular the North, is the proposed transport of plutonium between the United States and Japan. I think anyone would consider plutonium to be a toxic substance. There is a lot of concern about what Canada can and should do about that. This legislation does not particularly address that issue, of course, but I see nothing in it which would allow the Minister of the Environment to intervene. I realize that this also affects other Ministries, and that leads to my next point about the strength of this legislation with regard to coordination.
North of 60 there is probably no greater problem in environmental and industrial issues than the lack of coordination. Other speakers have mentioned that this Bill
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
reduces the number of laws from 58 to 55, but I do not think that will cause rejoicing in the general public. The lack of coordination is extremely confusing for both industry and individuals and leads to the most serious problem of lack of accountability and responsibility.
When there are 24 Departments and 55 laws involved, finding the committee, board or Department which will accept responsibility is virtually impossible unless one is a lawyer, and perhaps even then. This legislation does not send out a strong signal that the Government is committed to taking over the management of the environment, that it will not allow it to be destroyed but will spend a great amount of time and resources cleaning up the mess that has been allowed to develop. This is not an area in which mistakes are easily redressed. We have seen many examples of that, some of which other speakers have mentioned. This is an area in which we must anticipate as well as work. While there are some parts of the Act which do that, I am very concerned about the lack of co-ordination, the lack of one identifiable source which is committed to taking this on seriously.
I certainly agree with the preamble of the Bill which states that environment is one area which really is a federal national concern. Air pollution, pollutants in the soil, and pollutants in the water are no respecter of territorial, provincial or international boundaries. That is an area in which we must be very vigilant. I find that section particularly vague and hope the committee will find it within its purview to study it. North of 60, international relations concerning the environment, particularly with Greenland and the United States, are very serious, as many people here will know.
Again on the issue of co-ordination, there have been many recent examples in my own riding of problems with this. One example is the dumping of raw sewage into the Yukon River. Millions of tonnes were dumped before anyone knew about it. The reason given by one level of Government was that it did not want to alert the people downriver because they might get upset. Given that they drank the water that came downriver, you can be darned sure that they were upset when they eventually found out. There were a number of federal, municipal and territorial Departments involved in that issue. That illustrates the need for good communications, good coordination, and having someone in charge. I hope the committee will very seriously address the issue of co-ordination.
Environment is one of the issues which is closest to everyone. Everyone knows something about the environment and has some opinion on it. The more complex we make legislation, the more difficult we make the consultative or advisory process, the further we are from doing something meaningful about the environment. Although it is very important for the federal Government to take the initiative and the responsibility, it will only work if everyone participates in it.
1 will again use the health analogy. We can have very good health programs and a national medicare system, but unless people take some responsibility for their own health, these

September 17, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
programs are very difficult to implement. Therefore, the federal Government must send out strong signals of leadership in terms of proposed legislation.
I suggest that our success with enforcement and the public perception of the Government's commitment to enforcing environmental legislation has been undermined somewhat by our history. As an example, an article in the Edmonton Journal in April of this year reported the first ever conviction of a firm for Arctic pollution. There has been a lot of pollution in the Arctic, as many people will know. The judge in that case said that with the great potential for harm to the northern environment people in businesses operating in the northern extremes of Canada have a substantial burden to take precautions to protect the delicate balance of nature.
The fine in that case was $14,000. It was certainly a symbolic fine and I do not suggest that this was the responsibility of the federal Government. However, the public perception is that this issue has not been taken seriously. I believe that the public is looking for leadership and a strong commitment to the environment. While we support the step being taken by the Government in this legislation, I do not believe that it signals to the public the strong commitment that the public is seeking for the protection of all of us, our health, our agriculture, our water, and all that sustains us.
In Clause 5 of the Bill, the consultation processes, the establishment of advisory committees, and so on are being discussed. I realize that much of this is in the legislation, but I think that when these committees are being considered it is important to recognize that aboriginal people who have lived on and with the land, particularly north of 60, but in the south of Canada as well, have much to contribute to this consultative process. I hope that in some way this legislation, and the regulations in particular, will reflect that significant participation which would be essential to good and useful legislation.
In conclusion, I concur with my colleagues who have stated that this is a good first step. However, there are some amendments which should be made which we will propose during committee stage. I hope the Government will take a much stronger position and demonstrate to the Canadian public a political will to show leadership on environmental issues beyond this small piece of legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Member on her excellent speech. She touched upon some very important points. Enforcement is indeed a very important issue as is co-ordination, both of which she brought to the attention of the House.
The Hon. Member mentioned the enforcement mechanisms in Clause 5 and Clause 7. Clause 5 deals with advisory committees and Clause 7 deals with objectives, guidelines and codes of practice. The real enforcement clauses are Clause 100, Clause 101, and Clause 102 under investigation of
offences. Clauses 103 to 107 under offences and punishment are also very strong.
I believe this Bill is very tough in terms of enforcement when one considers the various punishments of offences that are outlined. I believe the Government should be congratulated for what it has brought forward in terms of punishment for those who pollute the environment.
Furthermore, individuals have various rights. There is the right of a person who has or may sustain a loss or damage as a result of action prohibited by the Act to seek an injunction from the courts to stop or prevent the action. There is the right of 12 persons to petition the Minister to investigate an alleged violation. The Minister must respond with his findings. There is the right of a person to have his or her identity kept confidential.
The legislation provides for fines of $1 million and the punishment of life imprisonment. The chief financial officers of companies can be subject to jail sentences. The enforcement sections of this Bill are very extensive, and I want to bring that to the attention of the Hon. Member who spoke very eloquently on a number of points. This Bill is very loud and clear in its enforcement sections. She may wish to review those clauses of the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have read the clauses which the Hon. Member has highlighted. I agree that they are good clauses.
My point is that we must ensure that there are sufficient resources in order to carry out those investigations and so that complaints can be promptly investigated and considered. However, I realize that that may deal with regulations more than the Bill itself.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is the New Democratic Party spokesperson on tourism. Would she give us some of her views about what this Bill will do for tourism?
We all depend on better environmental protection, but people in the tourist industry, including small business people and others, have a more immediate dependence on the environment being healthy in order to attract people to their part of the country.
Does she believe the measures in this legislation are adequate to take care of environmental pollution and will be welcomed by the tourist industry? Does she think that these measures will achieve the significant results they need? In other words, how beneficial will this be to tourism in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague has raised an extremely important point. During my speech I referred to the importance of the environment and economic development. I certainly include tourism potential in that area.
One of the difficulties with environmental issues is that many environmental problems are not readily identified. Therefore, it is important that experts in the area anticipate
September 17, 1987

these problems before the environment is too polluted to be restored.
While it is extremely important to preserve our environment for ourselves primarily, it is also important to take into account the enormous tourism potential of our environment. Many people visit all parts of Canada, not only the North, and come here to see the wilderness. They want a clean environment, with clean air.
For example, I talked to American tourists who came to the North and were awed by our clean environment and clean cities. That is one of the reasons that they visit us.
I believe in a Bill of environmental rights that guarantees a clean, healthy environment for all of us, not just to develop economic possibilities. However, a clean environment is certainly a consideration for economic development where tourism is concerned. It is extremely important to remember that tourism is a big industry in Canada and represents some 10 per cent of our employment.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the Hon. Member's comments with respect to the whole question of enforcement in this Bill and in environmental legislation in general. I was also interested in her concern about the commitment, including the commitment of resources, that is necessary if environmental legislation is to be actually enforced.
We know that there has been a great deal of criticism by various environmental groups and the public at large about the commitment and effort that has been made in the past by previous Governments in enforcing this kind of legislation. However, the Hon. Member referred to the one and only conviction for ocean dumping that was registered very recently in the Beaufort Sea near her own constituency. It was a conviction against the Gulf Oil Company, with a fine of almost $200,000.
I suggest that because this occurred recently for the first time, as far as enforcement of legislation in those Arctic waters is concerned, it is an indication that there is a commitment to enforce environmental laws, particularly those that deal with the area north of 60. Furthermore, the Minister announced in June a commitment of a further $37 million over and above the existing budget to be directed specifically toward that commitment to the enforcement of environmental legislation.
Would the Hon. Member not agree that there has been, specifically through that Gulf Oil prosecution and the further commitment of funds, a very substantial and positive indication on the part of the Minister and the Government that they are serious about the matter of enforcement of this legislation?

Mr. Speaker, the case to which I was referring occurred last spring, in which there was a $14,000 fine. However, the Member's point is well taken and I believe the examples he has given are positive ones. I hope we will see
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
more of them. It is the public's perception that such convictions have been limited in the past, and I hope the kinds of examples which the Hon. Member gives will increase so that we are not simply discussing one or two isolated cases.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to join in the debate on Bill C-74 as presented by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan). Matters relating to the environment are very important to the people of the City of Hamilton. The Department has indeed been very active and visible in the City of Hamilton over the last little while. It was just in January of this year that the Minister came to the city to open an energy-from-waste pilot plant located at the Canadian Centre for Inland Waters right on Hamilton Harbour. This is a very important and new technology. It is one which demonstrates a technique that imitates the natural process of oil synthesis by converting at least 90 per cent to 95 per cent of the carbon in the sludge to a usable form of energy. To date, approximately $3 million has been spent by the federal Government on this particular project.
The federal Government has also agreed to provide at least $1.25 million towards the clean-up of the Windermere Basin in Hamilton Harbour. That is being done as part of its international commitment to the Great Lakes Water Quality Board and the International Joint Commission. The Department of the Environment, in keeping with its theme of consultation, of course, has consulted with a 45 member stake holders' group to define uses of the harbour and to seek advice during the development of a remedial action plan to clean up the harbour.
Water is an important issue for Hamiltonians. As you know, Mr. Speaker, we border on one of Canada's Great Lakes and we are constantly reminded of the importance of this valuable natural resource. I want to speak today about the implications of Bill C-74 for the protection of water resources from environmental pollution.
There is an old saying with a lesson for us all: "You don't miss your water until the well runs dry". It is a fact that our fresh water resources, particularly along the Canada-U.S. border, are an overused and often abused resource. We depend on these resources for drinking water, recreational and industrial uses, and, of course, tourism. This is more true of Canada than the United States as 50 per cent of the Canadian population lives within the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence basins, whereas just 12 per cent of Americans live in the same area. Industries on the Canadian side of the border represent over 50 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product, and again the corresponding figures for the United States are much lower.
These national comparisons, however, contrast sharply with absolute statistics compiled on a regional basis. Americans consume six times as much water as Canadians in the Great Lakes Water Basin and are responsible, in my opinion, for a great deal more of the pollution that occurs in that area.

September 17, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Therefore, it is not surprising that support in this country, especially in the City of Hamilton, is strong for initiatives such as the Canada-U.S. Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement and the joint Canada-U.S. plan to monitor and reduce toxic loadings to the Niagara River.
It is also then understandable that the Government of Canada is anxious to put in place more effective national environmental protection legislation. The Minister of the Environment brought into Parliament on June 26, 1987, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act to begin the process towards legislative approval and enactment. This legislation is important for us in the City of Hamilton, and for all of Canada, because it does a number of things and 1 would like to outline just what they are. First it gives authority to control the introduction into Canadian commerce of substances, whether they be chemical, organic, inorganic, animate or inanimate that are new to Canada. It also gives authority to obtain information on and to require testing both of new substances and substances already existing in Canadian commerce.
It contains provisions allowing control of all aspects of the life cycle of toxic chemicals, including fuels, from development through manufacture or importation, transportation, distribution, storage and use, their release to the environment in such forms as emissions, and their ultimate disposal as waste.
It also contains provisions for regulations governing federal works and undertakings and for regulations to protect federal lands and waters within the legislative authority of Parliament where legislation administered by federal Departments or agencies does not provide for making regulations to protect our very important environment.
There are also provisions to create national objectives and guidelines setting desirable levels of environmental quality as well as release guidelines and codes of practice. The Act also allows control of sources of air pollution in Canada which would likely result in violations of international agreements or which affect another country, and where reciprocal legislation exists to control the sources of that pollution.
It contains provisions for control of nutrients such as phosphates in water conditioners or cleaning products which can interfere with the use of water by humans, animals, fish or plants. There are also provisions to issue permits to control dumping at sea from ships, barges, aircraft and man-made structures, excluding normal discharges from offshore energy facilities.
The Act also contains the authority for the federal Government to sign agreements with the provinces and territories of Canada for the administration of the legislation.
A lot of public attention has been given to the sections of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act that deal with toxic substances. We have been asked how the new Act differs from Canada's current legislation covering these chemicals. That legislation is called the Environmental Contaminants Act.
While both the Canadian Environmental Protection Act and the Environmental Contaminants Act are based on the criminal law power assigned to the federal Government under Canada's Constitution, the Environmental Contaminants Act is residual legislation. That means that under that Act, the Minister is obliged to ascertain whether action to alleviate the danger could be undertaken by other federal agencies or the provinces under their specific legislation. It is clearly back-stop legislation.
The new Act is pro-active and much broader in scope. The definition of "environment" contained in the Act is a clear indication of this breadth. In the context of the new legislation, "environment" means the components of the earth and includes air, land and water, all layers of the atmosphere, all organic and inorganic matter and living organisms, and the interacting natural systems that include components referred to in paragraphs of the Act.
With respect to its pro-active character, the new Act allows the federal Government to deal with substances at all points of their life cycle. For example, where the Environmental Contaminants Act had only limited provisions for submission of information on, and review of, new chemicals, the new Act has stringent requirements for submission of information on substances that manufacturers and importers are seeking to introduce to Canadian commerce for the first time. In contrast to the Environmental Contaminants Act, the new Act empowers the federal Minister of the Environment to do certain things, and this is extremely important: first, to issue orders prohibiting an activity involving a substance new to Canada where he or she has reasonable grounds to believe that the substance has been manufactured in or imported into Canada in violation of the Act; second, it empowers the Minister to make emergency orders to prevent release to the environment of a substance believed to be toxic where the substance presents a significant danger in Canada to the environment or to human life or health. It also empowers the Minister to issue orders requiring remedial measures to manufacturers, processors, importers, distributors or retailers. These remedial measures may direct an individual or a company to undertake such measures as giving public notice of any danger to the environment, human life or health, accepting return of the substance or product and reimbursing the purchase price to the purchaser, or recalling the substance or product and replacing it by one that does not present a danger to the environment, human life or health.
What are the implications of the new Canadian Environmental Protection Act for water and control of water pollution? Because the Act gives new authority to the Government of Canada, it can better control substances throughout their life cycle. This will ensure prevention of the release of harmful substances directly to water, from both surface and underground water sources and indirectly through emissions or from the land due to run-off, leachates, and so on.
Phosphates, as a nutrient, will be regulated under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act at the time of its
September 17, 1987

passage. Federal authorities may also consider controls for other nutrients such as organic carbon compounds if these substances are shown to have an adverse effect on the aquatic environment.
As I explained earlier, under the new Act, the Minister of the Environment is required to create environmental quality objectives, guidelines and codes of practice. While these objectives, guidelines and codes do not have the force of law, they will influence the direction and level of environmental protection efforts right across Canada.
Environmental quality objectives can apply to specific areas of Canada, or be clearly national in scope. In the short term, federal efforts will likely focus on inter-jurisdictional, that is, Canada-U.S., and interprovincial matters. Codes of practice may specify design operating and decommissioning procedures, or all of these for industrial and municipal facilities, as well as operations involving any form and handling of chemicals, disposal of wastes, et cetera.
Opposition Members in their contributions to this debate have been led astray in their observation that co-operation with the provinces in the protection of our environment will lessen the efficacy of the implication of this legislation. The Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), for example, suggested that what we need are strong national standards. He wants legislation that will be an imposition on the provinces and not one which is an agreed upon Bill by all parties involved.
The federal environmental authorities will consult with the provinces, as well as with industry, municipalities, labour, environmental groups, and all other interested parties across Canada on the development of these objectives, guidelines and codes. This is in keeping with Environment Canada's traditional approach of consulting first with affected stake-holders, such as provincial Governments and others, in order to understand their concerns and build consensus in both the process and the result.
This legislation is the environmental legislation which we believe will see us into the 21st century. It has the general support of industry which participated fully in the consultation process that over the last five years has led to the creation of this Bill. The preservation and maintenance of environmental quality are the shared responsibilities of Governments, industry and individuals. Canadian society now understands this and understands that further environmental quality is essential to protect Canada's resource-based economy and the many and varied in-stream uses of our virtually priceless water resources.
This Bill, along with co-operation and consultation with all Governments in Canada, is the tool for solving environmental problems and preventing those of tomorrow. This Bill is clearly good news for Canada, and especially good news for the City of Hamilton.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member pointed out quite correctly that the spokespersons for both the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party, joined by environmental organizations and the Canadian Labour Congress, have expressed concerns about a provision in the Bill which calls for consultation, and I suppose agreement, between the federal and provincial Governments before much can be done. They see this as a serious drawback to effective action being taken. I want to point out a specific case to the Hon. Member and ask him to tell us how he thinks we could deal with it.
We have in the Province of New Brunswick, which is a have-not province, a province in which a large percentage of its people are unemployed, one family, the Irving family, which controls virtually all the pulp and paper industry, the mining industry and the energy industry in that province. It has repeatedly, in its determination to maximize its profits, ignored recommendations, studies-and I am speaking from memory when I say this but I think I am correct-and court orders requiring it to improve its methods of operation so that it can begin to reduce the waste products which it dumps into the rivers of that province and the way in which it pollutes the water, the air and the earth of the province. That family has simply refused to do anything to move in the right direction.
I ask the Hon. Member how he thinks that, without a good deal of federal authority, that disgraceful situation in the Province of New Brunswick can be changed.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his questions. He has obviously asked several. The first thing I want to say is that the approach of the Government in federal-provincial relations is very much one based on consensus-building as opposed to confrontation, an approach that was adopted by the previous administration. He clearly knows that what we are endeavouring to do is to build a consensus so that all Canadians are onside with respect to matters relating to the cleaning up of the environment.
I think the Hon. Member would agree with me that the construction of regulations, guidelines and codes should be based on a program of consensus with the specific government bodies which have jurisdiction over matters concerning the environment, that is, both federal and provincial Governments.
In terms of the Hon. Member's reference to the Province of New Brunswick, I think the Hon. Member will agree that this legislation gives the federal Government authority to act. If he examines the penalties and the enforcement provisions in the Bill he will agree that once this legislation has been passed there will be significant penalties and clout available to address some of the matters he has raised.

Mr. Speaker, can the Hon. Member tell us how this Bill will clean up Hamilton Harbour? How will it respond to the stake-holders' concerns, the International Joint Commission?

September 17, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act

Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned earlier, the federal Department of the Environment has already made some significant improvements in terms of improving the quality of the water in Hamilton Harbour. I made reference to two of them at the beginning of my remarks. There is a commitment to spend SI.25 million on the clean-up of the Windermere Basin, as well as the energy from waste operation at the Canadian Centre for Inland Waters.
I think the Hon. Member will agree that the process of building a consensus toward cleaning up the environment, enforcement of the legislation and penalties, will now be available to the federal Government as a result of this Bill, specifically in terms of dealing with some of the problems that we are experiencing in the City of Hamilton.
It took the initiatives of the Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) as well as the Minister of the Environment to get these types of measures under way. We waited for over 20 years while the previous administration did not have the guts to bring forward a comprehensive environmental protection Bill.

Mr. Speaker, in terms of a body of water, Hamilton Harbour has been cited as one of the 10 most important trouble spots in North America. How can the Hon. Member stand up and talk about $1.25 million? What type of effect will that sum of money have on solving this very serious problem?

Mr. Speaker, the $1.25 million contribution by the federal Government was a contribution shared by the regional municipality and the province. It was the amount of money required to deal with cleaning up the Windermere Basin.
The Hon. Member should also be aware that there were 45 stake-holders and a remedial plan of action being developed with respect to Hamilton Harbour. The Minister of the Environment's commitment to the City of Hamilton and to some of the pollution problems we face is that when these remedial plans of action are available the federal Government will be there to deal with them.

Mr. Speaker, I am interested in the Hon. Member's remarks, specifically with respect to Hamilton Bay and the problems surrounding it. The federal Department of the Environment has been in place now for some 15 years. It dates back to 1972. I understand that the former Government, which was in power for some 12 years of that period of time, had nine separate Ministers of the Environment during those 12 years. Can the Hon. Member tell us what action was taken during that 12-year period with respect to Hamilton Bay?

Mr. Speaker, I just want to correct the Hon. Member. He referred to Hamilton Bay. The residents of Burlington refer to it as Hamilton Bay. We in Hamilton refer to it as Hamilton Harbour. I stated earlier that the federal Government has agreed to contribute to some of the plans
outlined by the municipality and the provinces. This Government and this Minister are taking some definite action in moving toward the eventual clean-up of Hamilton Harbour.
I am not aware of any programs during the past 12 years undertaken by the previous administration to attempt to address this problem, which is very important to all the residents of the City of Hamilton.

Reference has been made to Hamilton Harbour. I wish to ask the Hon. Member a question on a waterway a little further along the Great Lakes system in the Toronto area. Year after year there are beaches where no one is allowed to swim because of the pollution. We rely on Lake Ontario for our drinking water. I wish to ask the Hon. Member, what good will this Bill do when enacted for these serious problems regarding water quality and recreation, the ability to use the natural beaches that we have in the Great Lake system, particularly in the Toronto area?

I am certain that the Hon. Member is aware that there is a provision in the Bill where we will now be able to identify the substances fully. There is an additional $37 million to be spent in the Ministry of the Environment for enhanced inspection facilities and personnel. If the Hon. Member understands the provisions of the Bill, she will know exactly what is available to clean up that problem.

Mr. Speaker, I would have loved debating the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Peterson) on the sequence of events that led to the federal Government's final awakening to the difficulties in Hamilton Harbour.
The Hon. Member should be aware, since Hamilton Harbour abuts on our ridings, that there was a report tabled which was put together by the City of Hamilton and the region in which they sought from the city, the region, the province, and the federal Government a total package which would amount to approximately $4 million to lead to the clean-up in the Windermere Basin, which is in my riding.
The city and the region got together, because of the nature of the serious problem, and the fact that the International Joint Commission has stated that Windermere Basin is one of the most polluted bodies of water in North America. According to the IJC report, the basin itself contains PCB concentrations which exceed the Ministry of the Environment guidelines by up to 68 times. Immediately the City of Hamilton and the Regional Municipality of Hamilton-Wentworth agreed to contribute $750,000 to cover their portion of the clean-up costs.
Following that decision in September, 1986, the provincial Minister of the Environment, Mr. James Bradley, immediately agreed that the province would commit approximately $1.2 million. The Ontario Government immediately came in with a commitment. The federal Government and this federal
September 17, 1987

Minister, who made many promises that he was going to clean up the environment, refused to do so.
I have stacks of correspondence in my office where he suggested that he is studying the matter and looking at it. In fact it was not until I managed, as the Member for Hamilton East, to get the whole matter referred to the intelligent Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry that it was agreed the matter would be put before committee because the federal Government was stalling on its contribution.
Meanwhile, another relevant event entered the picture which in a positive manner changed the outlook of the Minister on the difficult situation in the Windermere Basin. It was called the by-election.
After the full Liberal caucus went to Hamilton, met with the Mayor, reviewed the evidence of the serious contamination and pollution in the Windermere Basin, and after the Hon. Member for Hamilton East convinced the committee Chairman, I must admit that he was very quick to accept the suggestion that there be a reference. The Regional Chairman wrote to the Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry seeking an opportunity to appear before the committee to present the case of the City of Hamilton. The Department of the Environment was dragging its feet on coming up with its portion of a mere, piddling, measly, miniscule $1.2 million to help clean up one of the most polluted bodies of water in North America. The by-election was called, and I am glad that the Minister finally agreed.
I was also glad to hear the Hon. Member for Hamilton West state that the Minister will be prepared to follow up on the recommendations from the stake-holders' report. I assume that that means the Minister will follow up financially. If the Minister is prepared to follow up financially, we on this side of the House will be looking for significant financial contributions from the federal Government far in excess of the rather piddling $1.2 million set aside to assist the city. The city and the region have taken the initiative in this area in completing their proposal to clean up the Windermere Basin.
The Windermere Basin is probably a microcosm of the whole problem that the Government faces in terms of credibility. The Minister of the Environment himself started his tenure by saying that environmental protection in Bill C-74 would be the strongest piece of legislation in the western world. In the same manner as the Government said it was committed to cleaning up the Hamilton Harbour and the Windermere Basin, we have seen foot-dragging. Surprisingly, and even shockingly, this is the fourth year of the Government's mandate. This is the first piece of environmental legislation to be introduced for second reading and debated in the House.
On the one hand, the Minister can say that he is committed to the environment and his Government makes it a priority, but the reality is that for three years in this Chamber we have not had a second reading debate on an environmental Bill at a time when the environment is one of the issues uppermost in the minds of most Canadians. That is not to say that there has
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
been no activity in the Department of the Environment. Unfortunately, that activity has been of a negative nature.
In November, 1984, we raised in the House the issue of the Canadian Wildlife Service. The Government and the Ministers of the Crown said that there was no problem cutting back on the Canadian Wildlife Service. It will not have any effect. In particular, the Canadian Wildlife Service was in the throes of researching and analysing the eggs of certain gulls and birds that flew over Lake Ontario in order to determine when toxic chemicals in the water and in the air actually caused cancer, mutations, and deformations.
The scientists felt that if they could see those conditions in the birds first, they would be able to predict what may happen to human beings if we do not start to clean up our act. The Canadian Wildlife Service was performing a valuable and critical service when one considers the present state of some of the Great Lakes. That service was cut back. The Minister said it was no problem, it is just a few scientists studying gull eggs. What difference does that make?
At the same time, the Government cancelled funding for the Guelph Toxicology Research Centre. One would think that the Minister would be proposing positive legislation to help clean up the environment, but instead he seemed to be more interested in moving on his own public relations campaign. We will remember when the Minister was flown to the Laurentians during some type of environmental conference. He absented himself from the conference in order to fly to the Laurentians to be filmed singing a song about the environment for Canada's Environment Week.
However, what happened when his scientists wanted to tell the story about what was happening with chemical and toxic chemical contamination? When one scientist-and I think it is the most notable example, Mr. Speaker-dared talk about contamination in the St. Clair River, he issued an order that scientists should keep their mouths shut, not because their information was incorrect or inaccurate, but because they were telling the truth, the truth was actually getting to the Canadian public, and the Canadian public was becoming rather concerned about it.
Instead, we have had a Government and a Minister who have neglected to tell the public about the real crisis we are now facing in our environment in terms of chemical contamination of air, water, and land. The Minister has neglected to bring forward positive legislation. While the Bill before us today is supportable, it is certainly in no way near the legislation which he claimed would streamline the system and be the toughest legislation in the western world.
In fact, it must be frustrating for people in the public who are trying to understand what legislation governs the water we drink, the air we breathe, and the factories in which we work.

September 17, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Let me refer to what I was rather stunned to discover. I know this will prompt the Hon. Member from Toronto to jump to his feet with his oft repeated question: "What did you do for the last 16 years?" I think the public is getting a little tired of that tune and would like to hear what the Conservatives are doing. In any event, I have presupposed the question and answered it in advance.
1 was rather stunned to discover that there are 24 federal Departments administering 57 environmental laws. It is no wonder that Canadians get frustrated when they want to find out if they can swim in their beaches or drink water. The Government is bringing in legislation which is supposed to streamline the law, but Bill C-74, as it now is, will result in 24 federal Departments administering 55 laws. Three laws will be merged into one law, which will give us 55 laws administered by 24 federal Departments.
However, it is a step forward, albeit a baby step; of course I have babies on my mind these days. It is not even a small step forward; it is a baby step for man and mankind, but we shall support it.
We support the fact that there will be a system to assess the impact of new chemicals on human health and the environment. This is one reason that I, as health critic, was so pleased to speak on the legislation. We believe that for any legislation to be effective, there must be in place a system to assess the ultimate impact of new chemicals on human health.
The shortcoming in this piece of legislation is that it will not deal with existing chemicals. In particular, if we consider the fact that fertilizers, weed-killers, and such chemicals are specifically exempted from the legislation, of course it is a cause for some concern. However, the Bill will allow for the assessment of 60,000 chemicals which are in use today.
If we look at the financial resources which have been set aside for this assessment, we wonder whether it is really practical to expect that with $2 million to $3 million being set aside in each of three Departments we will actually have the teeth to be able to assess 60,000 chemicals in use today and the chemicals coming on stream so quickly. In many cases it is almost impossible to keep up with them.
We also support the fact that the legislation will at least begin the process of allowing the public to understand what is happening with the chemicals in use today, but we are most concerned that the financial resources are simply not available.
We also believe, in respect of Bill C-74, that instead of just englobing a rather rambling preamble, the Minister should have lived up to his promise and his obligation to bring forth a legislative environmental Bill of rights. He has talked about it in the past. We were waiting for it to be in this piece of legislation. Frankly, he just did not deliver.
I am sure another point would interest those involved in the area of human rights as well as foreign policy for Canada. It is rather bizarre that we are bringing forth legislation which could set in place mechanisms to ban a chemical in Canada,
but there is no concurrent mechanism to ban the chemical for export to other countries, most specifically the Third World.
In other words, if we say that a certain chemical should not be used in Canada because it will cause cancer, mutations in the limbs of children born to women exposed to the chemical, or other health problems, it will also cause those health problems in other countries. We think it is immoral that Bill C-74 does not contain a requirement that any banned chemical should be banned for sale and production in Canada and for production and export abroad. For Canada to say that a chemical is good enough for the Third World but not good enough for Canadians is wrong. I am sure my colleague from Toronto would agree with that assessment and would support the amendments we will be bringing forward.
We are also very concerned about the issue of ministerial discretion.

For over three years, and this Government is now entering the fourth year of its mandate, this Government and this Minister have not attempted to introduce for second reading in this House any bill on the environment.
Mr. Speaker, no one can blame us for being afraid that the fact that the Minister wants to provide too much power and too much discretion for himself could create problems.
If we look at Section 29.4, we find that the Minister may waive any of the requirements for information to assess whether a substance is toxic if he considers that it is not needed. If a new chemical comes on the market and the Minister considers that there is no problem as the manufacturer is a good company which he knows and does not want to examine, he can waive the review process without any possibility of appeal by ordinary citizens. This is what frightens us. As the Minister has introduced no bill on the environment until now and has not had the courage to fight to protect the environment for the last three years, we do not want to provide him with any personal discretionnary powers now.
Elsewhere, in paragraphs A) and B) of subsection 37.2, we see that the Minister has a power of exemption to say that any chemical can be exempted from the regulations if he so desires. We find this a bit frightening as we do not trust the Minister in view of the way he is drawn his feet for the last three years and we do not want to give him too much discretionnary power.
As 1 have already said, Mr. Speaker, we shall support this Bill, but we shall also put him on notice that we are not satisfied with his speeches and his rhetoric and we would prefer more practical, substantive and financial action. The little he is now spending is not enough to protect our environment.
I shall have to close on these last comments.
September 17, 1987
