subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-EMPLOYMENT OF VISIBLE MINORITIES
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-EMPLOYMENT OF VISIBLE MINORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suspect that you will not recall the Buddy Evans case which occurred in Metropolitan Toronto in 1979 or 1980. Because it has been a number of years now, my own memory is somewhat hazy about the particular case. Buddy Evans was a Canadian black. He was not too highly thought of by the police department. He became a cause celebre as a result of a shooting which occurred when the police felt that Buddy Evans was perhaps going to do them some harm, and they shot him. As a result, an inquest was held.
That inquest touched off a great furore of marches, demonstrations and counter-demonstrations, some in support of the police department of Metropolitan Toronto and some in support of Buddy Evans. At that time, Metropolitan Toronto came as close as it has ever been in the time that I can recall to having racial violence. It was very disturbing. It led to some major and dramatic changes in our society, particularly in Metropolitan Toronto. It led to the creation of a number of race-relation committees in the community. In fact, each one of the six municipalities in Metropolitan Toronto established race-relation committees as a result of that situation. It led to the establishment, for the very first time in this country, of a civilian police complaint review board in Metropolitan Toronto.
You will recall that since we have come to this House, Mr. Speaker, the RCMP Act has been amended to provide for that same sort of mechanism for the RCMP. It provided as well for liaison committees to be set up between the visible minority communities in Metropolitan Toronto and the police department. It also provided for increased efforts to be made to try to establish and augment the numbers of visible minorities who were members of the Metropolitan Toronto Police Department. All of this was a reflection of the fact that there was systemic discrimination within the police department and, for that matter, within virtually all employment in our own municipality.
Systemic discrimination was the same kind of problem as that of stereotyping, for example, with which women have had a great difficulty over a long, long time. It was one of the reasons that women could not break into many occupations and many fields. We are delighted that the new Deputy Clerk of this House is a woman.
If there is one thing on which my Party, your Party, the Progressive Conservative Party, Mr. Speaker, is founded upon,
Adjournment Debate
surely it is the principle of equality of opportunity. That is why for the very first time ever in Canada the present Government introduced employment equity legislation for the purpose of dealing with federally-regulated companies. It is why for the very first time the Government introduced an affirmative action program for the Public Service and it is why for the very first time it introduced an affirmative action program as part of the contract compliance regulations with which a business has to comply when contracting with the federal Government.
This legislation and policies were based on the fact that women, disabled people, native people, and the visible minorities should all be given equal opportunity as far as hiring, promotion, training and pay is concerned. Included was the concept of setting targets to ensure equality of opportunity. That was not for the purpose of giving priority to people who were not clever or not the best or the brightest. It was for the purpose of stemming and stamping out systemic discrimination in our society.
In August of this year Treasury Board set targets for visible minorities for the Public Service for the very first time, and next June federally-regulated companies will have to comply with those same laws. What about the RCMP? What is their place in this? A study was done recently by Professor Jain of McMaster University. He reported that although 7 per cent of the population of this country are visible minorities and 45 per cent of the labour force are visible minorities, only 1.7 per cent of the federal Public Service are visible minorities, and the RCMP would not even tell Professor Jain who the visible minorities were or how many there were in the RCMP.
When I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) in this House if he could tell me why the RCMP would not give this information to a study of this sort, he said it was contrary to the Canadian Human Rights legislation. That shocked me, because after all this Government will require the private sector to provide this information. It will require by way of an affirmative action policy the Public Service of Canada to provide this information. Why, then, would the RCMP not provide it?
I would like to know from the Parliamentary Secretary tonight when the RCMP is going to comply with the law of the land. Why will the RCMP, in a concrete and forthcoming manner, not demonstrate whether or not there is equal opportunity of employment in the RCMP? It is only through providing that information publicly that we are going to know whether the RCMP complies with the law of Canada or not.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-EMPLOYMENT OF VISIBLE MINORITIES
speechtext:
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, Treasury Board affirmative action guidelines and the employment equity legislation constitute comprehensive government policy designed to eliminate discriminatory barriers in areas of federal jurisdiction and to improve the participation of

September 17, 1987
Adjournment Debate
qualified women, natives, the disabled and under-represented visible minorities in the workplace, However, I should point out that neither the RCMP nor the Canadian Forces are subject to policy direction from Treasury Board on affirmative action or to the equal employment legislation because of the unique nature of the jobs performed by these institutions.
It should be made clear that I am referring here to the regular member and civilian member categories of employees as opposed to the public servant. These institutions have, nevertheless, attempted in the past to design personnel policies and practices which are in keeping with the spirit and principles which apply elsewhere.
In the case of the RCMP, special affirmative action measures have been developed where a particular need has been identified. For example, the RCMP, because of its extensive involvement in policing rural and northern wilderness areas, has a well-developed native constable employment program. The force employs approximately 240 native special constables to assist in providing policing services to native communities in the eight provinces and two territories where the force serves under contract.
RCMP recruitment policies also ensure that women are recruited equitably in proportion to the number of women seeking to gain entry into the force. While the demanding physical nature of police work precludes disabled persons from becoming regular members, the RCMP has one of the highest employment rates for disabled persons among its public servants.
With respect to visible minorities, the RCMP does not currently have a formal affirmative action program. In the absence of such a program, the RCMP could not legitimately collect information on the racial background or ethnic origin of prospective recruits or current members. Thus, the RCMP, at this time does not have data on the number of visible minorities serving in the force.
The absence of formal affirmative action programs does not mean the RCMP has been inactive in the area. The RCMP has been a forerunner in the police community in its efforts to overcoming cultural barriers through the development of crosscultural training programs. The force has also been successful in overcoming the reluctance on the part of certain visible minority groups from seeking employment as police officers through its contacts with ethnic groups, as well as through the use of the ethnic press in its recruitment campaign.
On May 19, 1987, a report was made by Dr. Harish Jain of McMaster University to a congress of the International Society for Intercultural Training and Research in Montreal. Professor Jain found that visible minorities were underrepresented in most major Canadian police forces as compared to their representation in the communities being policed. On May 26, 1987, when appearing before the Committee on Multiculturalism, Professor Jain asked that the RCMP comply
with the employment equality legislation and collect statistics on the status of visible minorities in the force.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) has been made aware of Professor Jain's proposals. In keeping with the RCMP's commendable leadership in meeting the needs of visible minorities and in attracting recruits from their midst, every effort will be made to respond to Professor Jain's suggestions. I believe I can safely say that the RCMP recognizes the importance of Canada's national police force being representative of the Canadian mosaic and that appropriate initiatives will be developed where required to achieve this objective.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION-BELL CANADA RATE INCREASE APPLICATION MINISTER'S LETTER TO COMMISSION
CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION-BELL CANADA RATE INCREASE APPLICATION MINISTER'S LETTER TO COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I recently raised a question with the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) concerning a letter which she sent on behalf of Bell Canada to Bell Canada Enterprises and which has been objected to very strenuously by four organizations, namely, the Consumers' Association of Canada, the Canadian Business Telecommunications Alliance, the Public Interest Advocacy Centre and the Association of Competitive Telecommunications Suppliers, a group which does not often get together but which is extremely concerned with the Minister's interference in a hearing before the CRTC for Bell Canada rates.
When the Minister responded to my question, she actually dug herself in deeper. She did not agree to withdraw her letter, which is what these organizations have asked her to do. The letter itself is very clear as to the nature of the intervention. She says:
In accordance with this policy-
-which she cites-
-and provided that Bell Canada submits, as evidence, an audited verification that the costs associated with the temporary transfer of its employees to BCI are recovered fully by Bell Canada, I would be prepared to review any future decision of the CRTC, which failed to reflect these principles.
So, for example, were the Commission to establish or impute a level of compensation from BCI to Bell Canada that exceeded the audited costs directly and indirectly associated with these transfers, I would be prepared to recommend to the Governor in Council appropriate action-
The only action the Minister can take is to recommend that Cabinet overturn that decision. I understand that the letter was also sent to the chairperson of CRTC directly and it was submitted in the documents in Bell Canada's rate case.
This letter is, of course, totally unwarranted interference in a procedure which was already in progress. I note that the decision which the CRTC had previously made had gone against Bell Canada. Bell Canada was incorrectly told that it had to allow $25 million more for expenses on account of risk undertaking by Bell Canada International, the whole point being that one should not shunt a risky business, from which the profits would go to certain shareholders, to the consumers
September 17, 1987

who are the telephone subscribers in a monopoly service. That is a very fundamental principle as the Minister admits.
However, the decision was made by the CRTC. Bell Canada did not appeal that decision, which was an avenue open to it. Instead the Chairperson of Bell Canada Enterprises, Mr. de Grandpre, had a little chat with the Minister. As a result of that little chat the Minister came up with a very convenient letter, which is appended to the rate application. If the CRTC takes the Minister's advice, one of the results would be an additional burden of $25 million on the subscribers. That is very unfair.
There are other issues at stake as well. The Minister is interfering in the process. When the decision is made by the CRTC, it could then go back to Cabinet for a decision. At that point, the Minister is supposed to advise Cabinet as to whether or not it should uphold the CRTC. How can she give impartial advice to Cabinet in a matter on which she has already taken a position? How can she work with the CRTC, with which she is supposed to be dealing on a policy basis, when she is giving it a very strong hint that it had better make a certain decision?
Whatever the decision, she could be in trouble with the courts should she deal with the matter before Cabinet. If the consumers lose, they could go to the courts and ask that the decision be overturned since the Minister was involved in the case inappropriately. She has made it impossible to properly fulfil her role in this whole process.
The Minister's letter puts the CRTC in an impossible position. If it knuckles under and adopts Bell Canada's arguments, it will lose its credibility completely because it is supposed to be an independent agency. If it does not give in to the Minister, it will harm its ongoipg relationship with the Minister.
There are a number of unanswered questions. Why does the Minister want telephone consumer rates to go up by $25 million so that the Government of Saudi Arabia can get cheaper telephone service? If Bell Canada was not satisfied with the decision of the CRTC, why did it not appeal? If Bell Canada International needs a $25 million hand-out, why does it not apply for a government grant?
I am extremely disappointed with the Minister's decision in the first place, and the fact that she is digging herself in deeper. When I raised the question, she responded with a gratuitous insult that hers was a balanced letter which I only need read, suggesting that I would raise a question about her letter without having read it in the first place.
In the view of these organizations that are active in the area of rate setting and very knowledgeable about CRTC processes, the Minister has abused her position by attempting to intimidate the CRTC and dictate its decision on this issue.
Adjournment Debate
The Minister should be giving policy directions to the CRTC and has failed to do that in numerous areas of broadcasting policy and specialty services. She should abdicate the role of interfering in particular cases and take on the role of giving policy direction where it is needed. She has failed utterly to carry out her responsibility and is interfering in a most inappropriate manner in an independent regulatory agency.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION-BELL CANADA RATE INCREASE APPLICATION MINISTER'S LETTER TO COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member alleged in her question in the House on September 9 that the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) had improperly intervened in a CRTC procedure on the part of Bell Canada. This is simply not the case. I am surprised that the Hon. Member, given that she has had ample time to review the Minister's letter to the Chairman of Bell Canada Enterprises, would raise this matter again.
The Minister's letter refers Mr. de Grandpre to the forthcoming CRTC proceedings as the proper opportunity for this matter to be resolved. It goes on to clearly state that the Government supports the CRTCs role in ensuring that Bell Canada subscribers do not subsidize the competitive activities of Bell Canada Enterprises.
Furthermore, the Minister reminds the BCE chairman that the onus is on Bell Canada to provide information to the CRTC that would allow the Commission to make the most informed decisions.
I fail to see how the Hon. Member can arrive at the conclusion that the Minister has taken the side of Bell Canada. On the contrary, she has told Bell Canada that it must take this matter up with the CRTC, that the Government fully supports the CRTC's role in protecting the telephone subscriber from unfair costs, and that Bell should provide additional information to the Commission.
The role of the CRTC is clear and has in no way been affected by the Minister's correspondence. As the Minister pointed out in her return letter to the group which had written to her about the issue, the Commission has full authority to determine this matter according to its statutory responsibility, and she fully supports its duty to make an informed, objective assessment.
The Hon. Member is very familiar with the Bell Canada Reorganization Act, Bill C-13, which dealt with the principle of separating Bell's monopoly and competitive activities. This principle exists in part to ensure that telephone subscribers do not subsidize BCE's competitive activities. The Minister has been entirely consistent with this policy.
I think that on careful reading of the Minister's letter, it is clear that rather than somehow compromising the regulatory process, as some Hon. Members have implied, in fact the Minister has expressed a great deal of confidence in the

September 17, 1987
Adjournment Debate
regulatory process and that she has clearly stated her belief that the normal regulatory process is the appropriate form in which to resolve this issue.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES-NATIVE ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT-CONSULTATION PROCESS-MINISTER'S POSITION
SMALL BUSINESSES-NATIVE ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT-CONSULTATION PROCESS-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was on August 11 that I asked questions concerning native economic development and a certain consultation process launched by the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Valcourt). This process of consultation was to help develop a native economic development program within his Department. I want to take the opportunity now to raise some concerns about native economic development in general and its priority with the Government in particular.
I found it interesting that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight), in response to my supplementary question to him on that date, chose to quote an excerpt from a resolution passed by the Assembly of First Nations in June 1987. The Minister read in part:
Federal initiatives to date have further entangled the First Nations in a complex web-short sightedness and jurisdictional disputes. Federal Departments responsible for supporting First Nation's economic development are unable to effectively co-ordinate their activities.
Of course, that is all true. The Minister used that statement to justify the very narrow approach being taken to develop a plan for native economic development. It is interesting, however, to read what the Minister left out of that very same resolution. The same resolution from the Assembly of First Nations states in full:
The federal Government continues to give lip service to the ideas of local control, self-determination, comprehensive community planning and adequate resources to establish appropriate infrastructures at the community level.
It went on to say:
-that the Assembly of First Nations would prefer a Government wide review of federal support for native economic development rather than the consultation being planned by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion on the future of its native economic programs.
The resolution then goes on to suggest that what should be happening is that native people should identify the goals they want to achieve and the means by which to achieve those goals, including what funding would be required and what changes are necessary to existing policies and programs.
I do not think the Government can logically argue that we need anything less than a comprehensive approach. Consultation on DRIE's native economic development program is not sufficient. I argue that all programs of all Departments of Government which affect native economic development must be looked at. Indian people must be intimately involved in all aspects, actively participating.
It is clear that often one part of the Government does not know what the other is doing. Programs from one source can deliberately frustrate the efforts of another Department. For example, it is not possible to deny the link between postsecondary education and future employment and economic
development. Yet we know that the Department of Indian Affairs has put a cap on its post-secondary budget and students are being turned away from colleges and universities. I ask the Government, then, how it expects to provide the supply of Indian tradesmen, administrators, professionals and managers that are required. The Government knows, and it has revealed it in an important briefing note to the Minister, which states that effective delivery of devolved Indian programs, advances and local autonomy and increased employability are dependent upon effective training and education of Indians.
The statistics are supportive of that assertion. Some 140,000 natives will become eligible to join the labour force over the next 10 years. The problems this will create cannot be underestimated. Just to maintain employment rates at the present low levels will require 8,000 new jobs annually. Most of the new jobs will be required in rural areas where opportunities have, to date, been very limited. Operational and policy linkages between labour market programming and economic development will continue to be extremely important.
That deals with education, Mr. Speaker. Second, no one can deny the link between adequate infrastructure in a community and economic development. Yet all Hon. Members know that basic water and sewer services are lacking in the majority of Indian communities in Canada.
Third, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) has persistently refused to make available to Indian bands the employment funds that they were able to obtain under the former Canada Works program to build houses in their communities. The Canadian Jobs Strategy program is not in most cases applicable to Indian communities. Yet here is where unemployment is the highest.
When the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) was the Minister of Indian Affairs, he commissioned a task force on Indian economic development. It was to prepare a data base on the state of Indian economic development in Canada. The task force determined that economic development in all respects falls far short of the national average.
I would like to quote Douglas Sanders from the Faculty of Law, University of British Columbia, who said:
The failure to deal seriously with the questions of Indian economies is the
single most glaring failure of national policy in both the United States and
Canada.
I conclude by saying that what the Government is doing is conducting a very narrow review and avoiding consultation. Behind it all is the present motivation of how it can reduce expenditures in this area or, if I may put it in the euphemistic terms of the Government, how to stabilize economic development resourcing at present levels.
What the Government is trying to do is to save money and to hide behind the consultative process. In the long run it is denying Indian people the economic independence that they
September 17, 1987

need to run their own lives and to get out from under a system of dependency that robs them of their own dignity, political power and the right to have the control over their own lives that they are seeking in a wide variety of ways.
[ Translation]
Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development: Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat surprised that the Hon. Member would treat so offhandedly the consultation process announced on July 24.

The consultation process which was announced on July 24 is now being branded by the Hon. Member as not comprehensive enough. What is important for natives and what we have undertaken to do is to go to the grass roots, to seek from them their views regarding the economic development program which is administered by DRIE. The Hon. Member refers to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, to CEIC, and other departments that have an interest in economic development. That is the very reason these departments are also part of this consultation process. They are part of the review group which will be able to take into account the views of natives and possibly influence the report which will be submitted to me and from which I in turn will go to the Government with recommendations.
Adjournment Debate
In his statement, the Hon. Member has embraced a whole range of topics which are important to economic development for natives. Of course, I can appreciate the political reasons for the Hon. Member saying that our agenda is this and that. The fact remains that we are committed to working with natives to ensure that they can become economically self-reliant. It is promising to see the reception that the consultation process received from bands and tribal councils. I look forward to the results of the consultation process. If, under the previous Government a department was doing things which the other departments did not know, under this Government we work en unisson and we know what we do as a Government. Cabinet reviews the conclusions of this consultation process. I hope that we will come up with measures that will improve and render more efficient the programs that we wish to put in place to ensure economic development among natives in this country.
